learningPoints.description: Solid angle Ω = A/r² (steradians), by analogy with plane angle θ = s/r (radians); a full sphere subtends 4π steradians
If molecules are equally likely to travel in any direction, the fraction whose velocity lies in solid angle dΩ is dΩ/4π
For a chosen axis, the solid angle of the annular ring between θ and θ+dθ is dΩ = 2π sinθ dθ
Number density of molecules with speed in [v,v+dv] travelling at angle [θ,θ+dθ] to a fixed axis: n f(v) dv · ½ sinθ dθ
Volume swept out in time dt by molecules travelling at angle θ toward a wall of area A: Av dt cosθ
Flux formula: number of molecules hitting unit wall area per unit time with speed [v,v+dv], angle [θ,θ+dθ] is v cosθ n f(v) dv ½ sinθ dθ, integrated over θ∈[0,π/2] only
Pressure = perpendicular contact force / area of contact; unit pascal (Pa = N m⁻²); other units bar, atmosphere, torr
Equation of state p = f(T,V,N); the ideal gas equation pV = NkBT as one example
Momentum change per wall collision is 2mv cosθ; setting up the pressure integral p = ∫∫(2mv cosθ)(flux term) dθ dv
Evaluating the pressure integral using ∫₀^(π/2) cos²θ sinθ dθ = 1/3 to obtain p = (1/3) n m ⟨v²⟩
Kinetic-theory derivation of the ideal gas law: pV = (1/3)Nm⟨v²⟩, then using ⟨v²⟩ = 3kBT/m gives pV = NkBT
Equivalent forms of the ideal gas law: pV=NkBT; p=nkBT (n=N/V); pV=n_mRT with gas constant R=NAkB=8.31447 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Ideal gas pressure is independent of molecular mass: heavier molecules hit harder but collide less often, and the effects exactly cancel
Estimate the height of the atmosphere from p ≈ ρgh assuming uniform density (Example 6.1)
Compute the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP from pV = n_mRT (Example 6.2)
Kinetic energy density u = (1/2)nm⟨v²⟩ and its relation to pressure, p = (2/3)u (Example 6.3)
Partial pressure of species i in a gas mixture: pi = nikBT
Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture in thermal equilibrium is the sum of the partial pressures, p = Σpi
Compute the partial pressure of CO2 in air from mass fractions and molar masses (Example 6.4)
Convert pressure units and compute the molar volume of a gas at ultra-high-vacuum pressure (Ex.6.1)
Calculate the kinetic energy density u for air at atmospheric pressure (Ex.6.2)
Reason about what stays fixed (p) vs. changes (n) when a room is heated at constant pressure, and its effect on the total internal energy of the air (Ex.6.3)
Compute the pressure and volume of an interstellar gas cloud from its temperature, number density, and total mass (Ex.6.4)
Show ⟨cosθ⟩=2/3 for molecules hitting a wall, and contrast the mean energy of all molecules (3/2 kBT) with that of molecules hitting the wall (2kBT) — a flux selection-effect derivation (Ex.6.5)
Derive ⟨u⟩=0, ⟨u²⟩=(1/3)⟨v²⟩, ⟨|u|⟩=(1/2)⟨v⟩ for a Cartesian velocity component u by integrating the direction/speed distribution (Ex.6.6)
Show cross-correlations between distinct Cartesian velocity components vanish, ⟨vᵢvⱼ⟩=0 for i≠j, and verify by integration (Ex.6.7)
Alternative 1D-flux derivation of the ideal gas law and of the effusion flux Φ=(1/4)n⟨v⟩, using the single-component speed distribution g(vx) (Ex.6.9)
Compute the partial pressure of O2 in air from mass fractions and molar masses (Ex.6.8)
Molecular flux Φ = (number of molecules)/(area × time), units m⁻² s⁻¹; distinguished from heat flux (J m⁻² s⁻¹)
Integrating the directional wall-flux expression (from 6.1.6) over all v and θ gives Φ = (1/4) n⟨v⟩
Alternative flux expression Φ = p/√(2πmkBT), obtained by substituting n=p/kBT and ⟨v⟩=√(8kBT/πm) into Φ=(1/4)n⟨v⟩
Graham's law: effusion rate ∝ 1/√m, following directly from Φ ∝ 1/√m
Isotope-separation effusion-rate ratio for 235UF6 vs 238UF6 (Example 7.1)
Relative effusion rate of He vs N2 through a small hole (Example 7.2)
Compute the particle flux for N2 gas at STP (Example 7.3)
Effusion rate through a small hole of area A is ΦA, valid while the hole is small enough not to disturb the container's equilibrium
Knudsen method: infer vapour pressure from the rate of mass loss through a small hole (Example 7.4)

Knudsen flow: mass flow rate of gas down a long narrow pipe at low pressure, Ṁ ≈ D³⟨v⟩(p1−p2)/L (Example 7.7)
Find the residual-gas pressure that deposits less than one monolayer per hour on a clean surface (Ex.7.1)
Compute the mean kinetic energy of a Maxwellian gas and the final temperature of gas trapped after streaming through a small hole into a box (Ex.7.2)
Estimate the vapour pressure of mercury from a measured mass-loss rate through a small hole (Ex.7.3)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Collision model: a molecule moving at speed v through stationary molecules of cross-section σ sweeps out a volume σv dt in time dt, giving collision probability nσv dt

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Survival-probability recursion P(t+dt) = P(t)(1−nσv dt) leads to the differential equation dP/dt = −nσv P

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Solving the survival equation gives P(t) = e^(−nσvt), the exponential (Poisson) collision-time statistics

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Mean scattering time τ = 1/(nσv), obtained from τ = ∫t·(nσv)e^(−nσvt) dt

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Impact parameter b (the undeflected distance of closest approach) and the hard-sphere potential V(R): 0 for R>a1+a2, ∞ for R≤a1+a2

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Collision cross-section σ = π(a1+a2)² from the "swept tube" argument; reduces to σ=πd² for identical spheres of diameter d

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: The hard-sphere model is a good approximation at low temperature but worsens as temperature rises, since real molecules are "squashy" and their effective cross-section shrinks at higher collision speeds

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: A naive mean free path λ=⟨v⟩τ=⟨v⟩/(nσv) is wrong because it treats target molecules as stationary instead of using the relative velocity between colliding molecules

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Mean square relative speed ⟨vr²⟩=2⟨v²⟩, since the cross term ⟨v1·v2⟩=0 for independent molecules

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Approximating ⟨vr⟩≈√⟨vr²⟩≈√2⟨v⟩ gives the mean free path λ = 1/(√2 nσ)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Mean free path in terms of pressure, λ = kBT/(√2 pσ): at fixed temperature, λ is inversely proportional to pressure

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Compute the mean free path of N2 at room temperature and pressure (Example 8.1)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Compute the mean free path and mean collision time of N2 in a UHV chamber, compare wall collisions vs. intermolecular collisions, and see how these change at higher pressure (Ex.8.1)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Derive the rms free path (√2 λ), the most probable free path, and the fraction of molecules travelling further than λ, 2λ, 5λ, from the exponential free-path distribution (Ex.8.2)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Show that molecules hitting a plane boundary have travelled an average distance 2λ/3 perpendicular to the plane since their last collision (Ex.8.3)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: The mean free path and collisions
learningPoints.description: Estimate the mean scattering time and mean free path for atoms in a diffuse interstellar hydrogen cloud (Ex.8.4)
Viscosity η defined via shear stress τxz=F/A=η d⟨ux⟩/dz for a Newtonian fluid; equivalently the momentum flux Πz=−η ∂⟨ux⟩/∂z

Molecules crossing a z-plane last collided a distance λcosθ away and carry a momentum deficit −m(∂⟨ux⟩/∂z)λcosθ; integrating this over the directional wall-flux formula (6.1.6, θ∈[0,π]) gives Πz=−(1/3)nmλ⟨v⟩(∂⟨ux⟩/∂z)
Resulting kinetic-theory viscosity η=(1/3)nmλ⟨v⟩
η is independent of pressure, since λ∝1/n cancels the n-dependence
η∝T^(1/2), since η is independent of n and only ⟨v⟩∝√T remains; gases become MORE viscous when heated, unlike most liquids
Substituting λ, σ=πd², ⟨v⟩ gives the explicit formula η=(2/3πd²)√(mkBT/π), predicting η∝√m/d²
Validity condition L≫λ≫d: need λ≫d to neglect 3-body collisions, and λ≪L so molecules mostly collide with each other rather than the walls (a gas with λ≫L is a Knudsen gas)
Rotating-cylinder viscometer: torque balance G=2πr³lη dω/dr integrated across the gap gives η=G/(4πωl)(1/a²−1/b²)
Heat flux Jz=−κ∂T/∂z (Fourier's law), general form J=−κ∇T; κ has units W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
Applying the same λcosθ transport argument to thermal energy (using heat capacity Cmolecule per molecule) gives κ=(1/3)CVλ⟨v⟩, where CV=nCmolecule is the heat capacity per unit volume
κ is independent of pressure and κ∝T^(1/2), by the same reasoning as for viscosity; explicit formula κ=(2/3πd²)Cmolecule√(kBT/πm)
The naive relation κ=cVη doesn't hold precisely: fast molecules carry more kinetic energy but not necessarily more x-momentum, so heat and momentum transport aren't governed identically
Hot-wire method for measuring κ: Q=2πrJr integrated radially gives κ=Q ln(b/a)/(2π(Ta−Tb)); underlies the Pirani gauge for vacuum pressure measurement
Self-diffusion flux (Fick's law) for labelled molecules: Φz=−D∂n*/∂z, or in 3D Φ=−D∇n*
Continuity argument on a thin slab (flux in vs. flux out) gives ∂n*/∂t=−∂Φz/∂z, which combined with Fick's law gives the 1D diffusion equation ∂n*/∂t=D∂²n*/∂z²
General 3D diffusion equation via the divergence theorem: ∮Φ·dS=−∂/∂t∫n*dV ⟹ ∇·Φ=−∂n*/∂t ⟹ ∂n*/∂t=D∇²n*
Kinetic-theory derivation of D using the same λcosθ transport argument (now applied to n*) gives D=(1/3)λ⟨v⟩
D∝p⁻¹ and D∝T^(3/2), unlike η and κ which are pressure-independent; relation Dρ=η, since D and η differ only by a factor of ρ=nm
Diffusion of dissimilar species (D12) uses the combined diameter (d1+d2)/2 and the reduced mass 2m1m2/(m1+m2) in place of d and m
Simple kinetic theory ignores the persistence of velocity after a collision and correlations between velocity components — these cause the inexact numerical prefactors (e.g. the 1/3 in η, κ, D)
Eucken's formula κ=(1/4)(9γ−5)ηCV corrects for CV having both a translational part (C'V) and a non-translational part (C''V), each transported with a different weight, 5/2 C'V + C''V
Chapman–Enskog theory replaces the numerical prefactors in η, κ, D (e.g. 2/3π→5/16 for η) without changing their pressure/temperature/mass/diameter scaling
Compare the dynamic and kinematic viscosity of air and water to decide which fluid is "more viscous" by each measure (Ex.9.1)
Use the measured thermal conductivity of argon at STP to find its mean free path and effective atomic radius, and compare with an estimate from solid argon's close-packed density (Ex.9.2)
Derive η=Kρ⟨c⟩λ from kinetic theory, use it to explain Boyle's damped-pendulum-in-vacuum observation, and estimate the lowest pressure Boyle could have reached (Ex.9.3)
Find the torque needed to hold one of two closely-spaced rotating discs stationary in a viscous gas (Ex.9.4)
Assess whether measured argon viscosities at two temperatures are consistent with simple kinetic theory and the atomic diameter inferred from solid argon (Ex.9.5)
Derive Eucken's formula from CV=C'V+C''V, deduce γ for several monatomic noble gases from measured κ/(ηCV), and find the translational fraction of their heat capacity (Ex.9.6)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the thermal diffusion equation
learningPoints.description: Mathematical analogy: heat flux J=−κ∇T, particle flux Φ=−D∇n, and electric current density Je=−σ∇φ all obey the same diffusion-type equation

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the thermal diffusion equation
learningPoints.description: Conservation argument via the divergence theorem: ∮J·dS=−∂/∂t∫CT dV ⟹ ∇·J=−C∂T/∂t, where C=ρc is the heat capacity per unit volume

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the thermal diffusion equation
learningPoints.description: Combining ∇·J=−C∂T/∂t with J=−κ∇T gives the thermal diffusion equation ∂T/∂t=D∇²T, with thermal diffusivity D=κ/C
1D thermal diffusion equation ∂T/∂t=D∂²T/∂x²
Wave-like trial solution T∝exp(i(kx−ωt)) substituted into the 1D equation gives a complex wavevector k=±(1+i)√(ω/2D) (Example 10.1)
For a sinusoidal surface boundary condition T(0,t)=T0+ΔTcosΩt, the physical solution is T(x,t)=T0+ΔTe^(−x/δ)cos(Ωt−x/δ), with skin depth δ=√(2D/Ω) (Example 10.1)
Skin-depth solution properties: exponential decay e^(−x/δ), a phase shift of x/δ, and δ∝Ω^(−1/2), so faster oscillations penetrate less deeply
In steady state (∂T/∂t=0) the thermal diffusion equation reduces to Laplace's equation ∇²T=0; D drops out, but κ still sets the heat flux via J=−κ∇T
Steady-state 1D slab between two fixed temperatures gives linear T(x) and heat flux J=(κ/L)(T1−T2); defines thermal conductance (U value) and thermal resistance (R value/tog) (Example 10.2)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: Spherically-symmetric Laplacian ∇²T=(1/r²)∂/∂r(r²∂T/∂r) when T has no θ,φ dependence

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: Steady-state spherical solution T=A+B/r, analogous to an electrostatic potential of a point charge plus a constant (Example 10.3)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: Substitution T=T1+B(r,t)/r reduces the spherical diffusion equation to a 1D diffusion equation for B(r,t) (the "spherical chicken", Example 10.4)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: Solving for B via separation of variables with sin(nπr/a) modes gives B(r,t)=Σ An sin(nπr/a) e^(−D(nπ/a)²t), with An fixed from the initial condition using Fourier-sine orthogonality (Example 10.4)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: At long times the centre temperature is dominated by the slowest-decaying (n=1) mode, giving simple exponential relaxation; cooking/cooling time scales as t∝a²∝(mass)^(2/3) (Example 10.4 conclusion)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The thermal diffusion equation for a sphere
learningPoints.description: Steady-state heat loss from a warm sphere (e.g. a metabolising animal) into an infinite medium: rate=4πκa(T0−T1), proportional to radius a rather than surface area or volume (Example 10.5)
Newton's law of cooling: heat flux J=hΔT, proportional to the temperature difference via a heat-transfer coefficient h
Applying Newton's law of cooling to a cooling cup of tea gives exponential decay T=Tair+(Thot−Tair)e^(−λt), with λ=Ah/C (Example 10.6)
Convection (forced or free) and thermal radiation are separate heat-transport mechanisms not captured by a pure-conduction treatment
Prandtl number σp=ν/D=ηcp/κ, comparing momentum diffusivity (kinematic viscosity ν=η/ρ) to thermal diffusivity D=κ/ρcp
Using the corrected κ=(5/2)ηcV and cp/cV=γ=5/3 for an ideal monatomic gas gives σp=2/3
σp≫1 means convection (momentum diffusion) dominates heat transport; σp≪1 means conduction dominates
A heat source H (W/m³) modifies the thermal diffusion equation to ∂T/∂t=D∇²T+H/C
Steady-state temperature profile of a uniformly-heated current-carrying bar with fixed end temperatures: T=T0+Hx(L−x)/2κ, peaking at the centre at T0+HL²/8κ (Example 10.7)
Particle diffusion obeys the same equation ∂n/∂t=D∇²n by direct analogy with heat diffusion

Steady-state absorption of particles by a perfectly-absorbing sphere gives an absorption rate 4πDan0, proportional to radius rather than surface area or volume — sets a maximum size limit for oxygen-absorbing organisms like bacteria (Example 10.8)

Find the decay length of sinusoidal temperature oscillations propagating into a semi-infinite solid, and use it to estimate daily/annual temperature swings (and their timing) inside an underground cellar (Ex.10.1)
Derive the steady-state radial temperature profile in a current-carrying cylindrical wire with fixed surface temperature, then redo it with a Newton's-law-of-cooling boundary condition (Ex.10.2)
Show that the centre of the spherical chicken reaches 90% of its final temperature after t∼a²ln20/π²D (Ex.10.3)

Derive the 1D heat-loss equation for a cooling fin (a cylindrical rod combining axial conduction with Newton's-law surface loss), solve for the steady-state profile of an infinite rod, and show the heat removed scales as a^(3/2) (Ex.10.4)
A thermodynamic system and its surroundings; thermal equilibrium means macroscopic observables have stopped changing with time, defining a particular equilibrium state
A function of state has a well-defined value for each equilibrium state, independent of how that state was reached; it has an exact differential df, with Δf=f(xf)−f(xi) path-independent
xy is an exact differential (Δf=1 along any path from (0,0) to (1,1)), while y dx is inexact (Δg is path-dependent) (Example 11.1)
Extensive (e.g. energy, volume, mass) vs. intensive (e.g. temperature, pressure, density) functions of state; an equation of state f(p,V,T)=0 connects them
Historical route to the first law: Lavoisier's caloric theory, Rumford's friction experiments, and Joule's mechanical-equivalent-of-heat measurements established that heat is a form of energy
The first law of thermodynamics: energy is conserved, and heat and work are both forms of energy; internal energy U is a function of state
Sign convention and first law: ΔU=ΔQ+ΔW (ΔQ>0 = heat supplied to the system, ΔW>0 = work done on the system), or differentially dU=đQ+đW with inexact differentials đQ, đW
A thermally isolated system cannot exchange heat, so ΔU=ΔW
Work done compressing a gas reversibly: đW=−p dV, from F=pA and A dx=−dV
Heat capacity at constant volume CV=(∂Q/∂T)_V=(∂U/∂T)_V, from dU=(∂U/∂T)_V dT+(∂U/∂V)_T dV at fixed V
Heat capacity at constant pressure Cp=(∂Q/∂T)_p, giving Cp−CV=[(∂U/∂V)_T+p](∂V/∂T)_p
Specific heat capacities cV=CV/M, cp=Cp/M (per unit mass)
For an ideal monatomic gas, U=(3/2)RT depends only on T, so (∂U/∂V)_T=0, giving Cp−CV=R, CV=(3/2)R, Cp=(5/2)R per mole (Example 11.2)
dU=CV dT holds for an ideal gas (since (∂U/∂V)_T=0) but not in general for a non-ideal gas (Example 11.3)
Adiabatic index γ=Cp/CV
γ=5/3 for an ideal monatomic gas (Example 11.4)
Internal energy per unit mass ũ=p/[ρ(γ−1)] and per unit volume u=p/(γ−1), using CV=R/(γ−1) (Example 11.5)
Explain why ΔU=0 in an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, then compute the work done by the gas and the heat flow into it (Ex.11.1)
Show that R/CV=γ−1 and R/Cp=(γ−1)/γ for an ideal gas (Ex.11.2)
Evaluate a line integral of dz=2xy dx+(x²+2y)dy along two different paths and determine whether dz is an exact differential (Ex.11.3)
Diagnose the apparent paradox that two "obviously true" calculations of ∂x/∂r in polar coordinates give different answers (Ex.11.4)
Critique the claim "heat is work and work is heat" as a summary of the first law (Ex.11.5)
Microscopic physics is reversible, yet everyday macroscopic processes (an egg breaking, a resistor dissipating heat) appear irreversible

100-coin box: ~10^30 microstates exist but only one is "all heads", while ~4×10^27 correspond to 50/50 — shaking almost always randomizes an ordered start, giving a statistical origin for irreversibility (Example 12.1)
A quasistatic process changes infinitesimally slowly, remaining in equilibrium throughout; fast changes (e.g. shock waves) convert energy irreversibly into heat
Reversibility requires the absence of friction/dissipation but does not exclude heat being absorbed or emitted; a reversible process can be run in reverse

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Isothermal ⟹ ΔT=0 ⟹ ΔU=0 for an ideal gas (since U depends only on T) ⟹ đW=−đQ

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Heat absorbed during a reversible isothermal expansion of 1 mole of ideal gas from V1 to V2: ΔQ=∫p dV=RT ln(V2/V1)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Adiabatic = adiathermal (đQ=0) AND reversible; then dU=đW

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: For 1 mole of ideal gas, CV dT=−RT/V dV integrates to ln(T2/T1)=−(R/CV)ln(V2/V1)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Using γ=1+R/CV, this becomes TV^(γ−1)=constant, equivalently p^(1−γ)T^γ=constant and pV^γ=constant

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: On a p–V diagram, adiabats are always steeper than isotherms at a given point
Combining the hydrostatic equation dp=−ρg dz with the ideal gas law gives T dp/p=−(mg/kB) dz
For an adiabatic (rather than isothermal) atmosphere, combining with p^(1−γ)T^γ=constant gives the adiabatic lapse rate dT/dz=−Mmolar g/Cp — a linear temperature decrease with height
The dry-air adiabatic lapse rate (~9.7 K/km) exceeds the observed atmospheric value (~6–7 K/km), due to moisture and latent-heat effects
Derive pVγ=constant, TV^(γ−1)=constant, and T=constant×p^(1−1/γ) for an adiabatic ideal-gas expansion (Ex.12.1)
For a general gas obeying pV=f(T), derive (∂p/∂T)_V and (∂V/∂T)_p in terms of df/dT, then use the adiabatic condition đQ=0 to re-derive pVγ=constant (Ex.12.2)
From đQ=CpdT+Adp=CVdT+BdV, derive (Cp−CV)dT=BdV−Adp and the adiabatic-vs-isothermal slope relations on a p–V diagram (Ex.12.3)
Relate the gradients of adiabats and isotherms on a p–V diagram using the slope relation from Ex.12.3 (Ex.12.4)
Find the final gas temperature after two different quasi-static gas-transfer operations between two insulated, valve-connected cylinders (Ex.12.5)
Rüchhardt's method for measuring γ: show a ball oscillating in a tube attached to a gas container undergoes SHM with period τ=2π√(mV/γpA²), plus Rinkel's drop-distance variant (Ex.12.6)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Clausius' statement of the second law: no process's sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Kelvin's statement of the second law: no process's sole result is the complete conversion of heat into work

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: An engine is a cyclic process converting heat into work; the Carnot cycle consists of two reversible adiabats and two reversible isotherms between reservoirs at Th and Tl, with W=Qh−Ql (first law, ΔU=0 around a cycle)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: For an ideal-gas Carnot cycle, combining the isothermal heat exchanges with the adiabatic T–V relations on each leg gives Qh/Ql=Th/Tl (Example 13.1)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Engine efficiency η=W/Qh<1, since the work out cannot exceed the heat in

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Carnot efficiency ηCarnot=1−Tl/Th, from W=Qh−Ql and Qh/Ql=Th/Tl (Example 13.2)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: A power-station steam turbine's Carnot efficiency (~60% between 800K and 300K) vs. its typical real efficiency (~40%) (Example 13.3)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Carnot's theorem: of all heat engines working between two given temperatures, none is more efficient than a Carnot engine

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Proof by contradiction: connecting a hypothetically more-efficient engine to a reversed Carnot engine would net-transfer heat from cold to hot with no other effect, violating Clausius' statement

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.description: Corollary: all reversible engines operating between the same two temperatures have the same (Carnot) efficiency

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Equivalence of Clausius' and Kelvin's statements
learningPoints.description: A Kelvin-violator connected to a Carnot engine can be shown to net-transfer heat from cold to hot with no other effect — i.e. it implies a Clausius violation

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Equivalence of Clausius' and Kelvin's statements
learningPoints.description: A Clausius-violator connected to a Carnot engine can be shown to net-convert heat entirely into work — i.e. it implies a Kelvin violation; together these prove the equivalence of the two statements

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Heat engines and the second law
