Entropy is defined by dS=đQrev/T; since ∮đQrev/T=0 for a Carnot cycle, đQrev/T is an exact differential and S is a function of state
A reversible adiabatic (đQrev=0) process is isentropic: it involves no change in entropy
Applying the Clausius inequality to a loop with one irreversible leg (A→B) and one reversible leg (B→A) gives dS≥đQ/T in general, with equality only for a reversible process
For a thermally isolated system (đQ=0), dS≥0 — another statement of the second law: the entropy of an isolated system tends to a maximum
Applied to the Universe as an isolated system: U_Universe is constant, while S_Universe can only increase
A small system reaching thermal contact with a large reservoir: ΔS_system and ΔS_reservoir can each be positive or negative, but ΔS_Universe=ΔS_system+ΔS_reservoir≥0 always (Example 14.1)
Combining dU=đQ+đW with đQ=TdS and đW=−pdV (both valid for reversible changes) gives dU=TdS−pdV; since every term is a function of state, this equation holds for irreversible changes too
U's natural variables are its extensive variables S and V; T=(∂U/∂S)_V and p=−(∂U/∂V)_S, and the reciprocity theorem gives p/T=(∂S/∂V)_U
Two systems exchanging internal energy ΔU and volume ΔV: ΔS=(1/T1−1/T2)ΔU+(p1/T1−p2/T2)ΔV, so equilibrium (ΔS=0) requires T1=T2 and p1=p2 (Example 14.2)
Joule expansion setup: a thermally isolated ideal gas expands into a vacuum; ΔU=0 implies ΔT=0 for an ideal gas, so the pressure halves when the volume doubles

Since the Joule expansion's path is undefined (non-equilibrium), its entropy change is instead computed along a reversible isothermal expansion between the same endpoints (S being a function of state); this gives ΔS=R ln2 for one mole

Entropy accounting for the Joule expansion vs. an equivalent reversible isothermal expansion: ΔS_gas=R ln2 in both, but ΔS_surroundings and ΔS_Universe differ — 0 for the reversible case, R ln2 for the irreversible Joule expansion (Example 14.3)
Resolving the apparent paradox that đQ=0 in the Joule expansion yet ΔS=R ln2>0: đQ=TdS only holds for reversible changes; in general đQ≤TdS
Comparing 1/T=(∂S/∂U)_V (from the first law) with the statistical definition of temperature motivates the identification S=kB lnΩ
Applying S=kB lnΩ directly to the Joule expansion (a 2^NA-fold increase in microstate count) recovers ΔS=R ln2 (Example 14.4)

Entropy of mixing of two distinguishable ideal gases at the same p,T: ΔS=−NkB(x ln x+(1−x)ln(1−x)), derived by treating the mixing as two independent reversible isothermal sub-expansions into the combined volume
The entropy of mixing is zero at x=0 or 1 and maximal at x=1/2 (ΔS=NkB ln2), matching the 2^N-fold increase in microstate count at equal mixing
Distinguishability is essential to the entropy of mixing: mixing two samples of the *same* gas produces no entropy increase, even though mixing distinguishable gases does
Maxwell's demon: a hypothetical creature that selectively lets molecules through a trapdoor appears to decrease entropy (e.g. reversing a Joule expansion) while doing no pdV work

Resolution: the demon must store (and eventually erase) information to operate, and erasing information carries an unavoidable entropy cost that compensates any entropy decrease it achieves in the gas

Total entropy decomposes as Stot=S+Smicro, where S is the entropy of measurable macrostates and Smicro=ΣPiSi (with Si=kB ln ni) is the entropy hidden in each macrostate's unmeasured microstates (Example 14.5)
This decomposition, combined with Pi=ni/N, leads to Gibbs' expression for entropy: S=−kBΣPi ln Pi
For equally-likely microstates (Pi=1/Ω), Gibbs' formula reduces to S=kB lnΩ (Example 14.6)
Maximizing Gibbs' entropy subject to ΣPi=1 and ΣPiEi=U via Lagrange multipliers recovers the Boltzmann distribution Pi=e^(−βEi)/Z (Example 14.7)
Compute the entropy decrease of cooling tea and comment on the sign, given that the tea is not an isolated system (Ex.14.1)
Reconcile "ΔQ=0, ΔW=0, yet ΔS=R ln2>0" in a free (Joule) expansion with the relation dU=TdS−pdV (Ex.14.2)
Compute the entropy change of a resistor and of the Universe from resistive (Joule) heating at fixed temperature (Ex.14.3)
Compare the entropy changes of a bath and a reservoir when heated by direct thermal contact versus via an intervening Carnot engine (Ex.14.4)
Compute the entropy change of cooling a block via a single bath versus two intermediate baths, and show the total entropy change vanishes with infinitely many intermediate baths (Ex.14.5)
Compute the entropy change of the Universe for charging/discharging a capacitor and for reversible vs. free gas expansions (Ex.14.6)
Compute the entropy change of an ideal gas and of a van der Waals gas under reversible-isothermal and free expansion, including the resulting temperature drop for the van der Waals case (Ex.14.7)
Show S/kB=lnZ+βU starting from Pi=e^(−βEi)/Z (Ex.14.8)
Derive the entropy-of-mixing formula directly from the Gibbs entropy expression (Ex.14.9)
The information content of a statement is Q=−k log P (less probable ⟹ more informative); information is additive for independent statements, matching how their probabilities multiply
The Shannon entropy S=⟨Q⟩=−kΣPi log Pi is the average information content of a set of outcomes
Shannon entropy of a fair six-sided die (2.58 bits) vs. a biased die weighted toward one outcome (2.16 bits) — less uncertainty gives lower entropy (Example 15.1)
Shannon entropy of a Bernoulli trial, S=−P log P−(1−P)log(1−P), maximized at P=1/2 and zero at P=0 or 1 (Example 15.2)
The Shannon entropy formula is identical (up to the choice of constant) to Gibbs' thermodynamic entropy — thermodynamic entropy measures our uncertainty about which microstate a system occupies
Landauer's principle: erasing N bits of stored information is irreversible and reduces the system's entropy by NkB ln2, so at least kBT ln2 of heat per bit must be dissipated into the surroundings
This resolves Maxwell's demon: the demon must eventually erase its memory, and the entropy cost of that erasure outweighs (or at best equals) the entropy reduction it achieves in the gas
A fair bit (P=1/2) cannot be compressed, but skewed probabilities (P≠1/2) allow lossless compression by giving short codes to common patterns and long codes to rare ones
A pairwise-bit compression scheme for P(0)=0.9 that saves bits on average, since the common pair "00" gets the shortest code (Example 15.3)
Shannon's noiseless channel coding theorem: a source with entropy S can be reliably compressed to rate R if R>S, but not if R<S — entropy sets the ultimate compression limit
The quantum density matrix ρ=ΣPi|ψi⟩⟨ψi| describes a statistical mixture of quantum states; ⟨Â⟩=Tr(Âρ) and Trρ=1; a pure state has ρ=|ψ⟩⟨ψ|, otherwise the state is mixed
The von Neumann entropy S(ρ)=−Tr(ρ log ρ)=−Σλi log λi (λi = eigenvalues of ρ) is the quantum generalization of Shannon entropy
The entropy of a pure state is zero; entropy is maximized (=log n) when all eigenvalues are equal, λi=1/n (Example 15.4)
Qubits, superposition, and entanglement have no classical counterpart; for an overall pure state, the entropy of a subsystem quantifies its degree of entanglement with the rest
Conditional probability P(A|B) and joint probability P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A); independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)
Law of total probability: P(X)=ΣᵢP(X|Ai)P(Ai), for mutually exclusive events Ai summing to probability 1
Bayes' theorem: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), relating the prior probability P(A) to the posterior probability P(A|B)
Drug-testing problem: a 95%-accurate test applied to a rare (1%) condition gives only a 16% posterior probability of guilt given a positive result (Example 15.5)

The "Mrs Trellis" problem: updating the probability of a family's sex composition on the information "one child is a boy" gives 2/3, showing how sensitive conditioning is to exactly what information is given (Example 15.6)
Compare a microchip bit's stored energy (in eV) to the minimum Landauer erasure heat kBT ln2 per bit (Ex.15.1)
Compute the Shannon entropy of the inputs/outputs of a reversible (NOT/NOT) logic gate and an irreversible (OR/AND) logic gate, and identify the crucial difference (Ex.15.2)
Maximize the Shannon entropy subject to a general constraint ⟨f(x)⟩ via Lagrange multipliers, deriving the general distribution Pi∝e^(−βf(xi)) and its partition function (Ex.15.3)
Derive the entropy S=−P log P−(1−P)log(1−P) for a bit-flip noise channel and its relation to the channel capacity R=1−S (Ex.15.4)
Define the relative entropy (KL divergence) S(P||Q), show S(P||Q)≥0, and use it to prove the maximum-entropy bound SP≤log N (Ex.15.5)
The Monty Hall problem: determine whether a game-show contestant should switch doors after a reveal (Ex.15.6)
U's natural variables are S and V (from dU=TdS−pdV); T=(∂U/∂S)_V and p=−(∂U/∂V)_S
For a reversible isochoric process, dU=đQrev=CV dT, so ΔU=∫CV dT (valid only at constant volume)
Enthalpy H=U+pV; dH=TdS+Vdp, with natural variables S and p
For a reversible isobaric process, dH=đQrev=Cp dT, so ΔH=∫Cp dT — enthalpy represents the heat absorbed at constant pressure
T=(∂H/∂S)_p and V=(∂H/∂p)_S, from dH=TdS+Vdp
Helmholtz function F=U−TS; dF=−SdT−pdV, with natural variables T and V
At constant T, ΔF=−∫p dV equals the reversible work done on the system; F is minimized at equilibrium under fixed T,V
S=−(∂F/∂T)_V and p=−(∂F/∂V)_T, from dF=−SdT−pdV
Gibbs function G=H−TS; dG=−SdT+Vdp, with natural variables T and p
G is conserved (dG=0) at fixed T,p; S=−(∂G/∂T)_p and V=(∂G/∂p)_T
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equations, U=−T²∂(F/T)/∂T and H=−T²∂(G/T)/∂T (Example 16.1)

The availability A=U+p0V−T0S generalizes free energy for a system exchanging heat/work with a reservoir at T0,p0; dA≤0 for any spontaneous change (second law), so equilibrium is reached by minimizing A
Which potential to minimize depends on the constraint: maximize S when isolated; minimize F at fixed T,V; minimize G at fixed T,p
Chemical reactions at constant T,p proceed spontaneously if ΔG<0; ΔH is the heat absorbed (exothermic/endothermic) but does not alone determine spontaneity (Example 16.2)
Requiring mixed partial derivatives to be equal (since each potential's differential is exact) yields a Maxwell relation from each of U, H, F, and G
The four Maxwell's relations, each connecting a hard-to-measure entropy derivative to an easier-to-measure p–V–T derivative
Maxwell's relations are best derived on demand rather than memorized; a mnemonic pairs conjugate variables (T–S, p–V) diagonally across each relation

Toolkit for thermodynamic derivations: write df in its natural variables, apply a Maxwell relation, invert with the reciprocal theorem (∂x/∂z)_y=1/(∂z/∂x)_y, or combine with the reciprocity theorem (∂x/∂y)_z(∂y/∂z)_x(∂z/∂x)_y=−1
Generalized susceptibilities: isobaric/adiabatic expansivity βp=(1/V)(∂V/∂T)_p, βS=(1/V)(∂V/∂T)_S, and isothermal/adiabatic compressibility κT=−(1/V)(∂V/∂p)_T, κS=−(1/V)(∂V/∂p)_S
(∂Cp/∂p)_T=−T(∂²V/∂T²)_p and (∂CV/∂V)_T=T(∂²p/∂T²)_V, both zero for an ideal gas (Example 16.4)
Cp−CV=VTβp²/κT, derived from S=S(T,V) combined with a Maxwell relation and the reciprocity theorem (Example 16.5)
Entropy of an ideal gas, S=CV lnT+R lnV+constant, from S=S(T,V) and a Maxwell relation (Example 16.6)
κT/κS=γ, proved via Maxwell's relations plus the reciprocal/reciprocity theorems, and verified directly for an ideal gas via pVγ=constant (Example 16.7)
Write down U,H,F,G and their differentials from dU=TdS−pdV, and derive all four Maxwell's relations (Ex.16.1)
Derive the general relations for (∂T/∂V)_U, (∂T/∂V)_S, and (∂T/∂p)_H, identify which type of expansion each governs, and verify their ideal-gas limits (Ex.16.2)
Derive (∂U/∂V)_T=(Cp−CV)/(Vβp)−p from the first law (Ex.16.3)
Show that knowing U(S,V) gives simple expressions for T and p, but knowing U(T,V) instead gives a much messier expression for p involving an unknown function of V (Ex.16.4)
Derive the general result p=T(∂p/∂T)_V−(∂U/∂V)_T (Ex.16.5)
Show S=Cp lnT−R lnp+constant for an ideal gas (Ex.16.6)
Show S=CV ln(p/ργ)+constant for an ideal gas (Ex.16.7)
Generalized force/displacement framework đW=X dx (e.g. gas: −pdV; elastic rod: f dL; liquid film: γ dA; dielectric: −pE·dE; magnet: −m·dB)
Isothermal Young's modulus ET=(L/A)(∂f/∂L)_T; linear expansivity at constant tension αf=(1/L)(∂L/∂T)_f, positive for metals but negative for rubber
(∂f/∂T)_L=−AETαf (Example 17.1) — explains why a heated metal wire held at fixed length slackens
First law for an elastic rod, dU=TdS+fdL; from the Helmholtz function dF=−SdT+fdL, S=−(∂F/∂T)_L and f=(∂F/∂L)_T
Maxwell relation (∂S/∂L)_T=−(∂f/∂T)_L=AETαf: stretching a metal wire (αf>0) isothermally increases its entropy and absorbs heat ΔQ=AETTαfΔL, while stretching rubber (αf<0) emits heat
(∂U/∂L)_T=f+ATETαf for an elastic rod — unlike an ideal gas, U changes on isothermal extension because the work done and the heat absorbed don't exactly cancel (Example 17.2)
Laplace's law for a droplet, p=2γ/r, derived by equating the mechanical work of expansion (p dV) to the surface-energy cost (γ dA)
Pressure inside a soap bubble (which has two surfaces) is pbubble−p0=4γ/r (Example 17.3)
Microscopic origin of surface tension: surface molecules have fewer attractive neighbours than bulk molecules, so creating a surface costs energy
First law for a surface, dU=TdS+γdA; the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂A)_T=−(∂γ/∂T)_A gives (∂U/∂A)_T=γ−T(∂γ/∂T)_A
Heat ΔQ=−TΔA(∂γ/∂T)_A>0 is absorbed on isothermally stretching a surface, since surface tension typically decreases with temperature
Work supplied to an electric dipole, đW=−pE·dE, combining the interaction energy with the field and the internal "spring" energy of stretching the dipole
The analogous result for a magnetic dipole is đW=−m·dB
First law for a paramagnet, dU=TdS−mdB; magnetic susceptibility χ=lim_(H→0) M/H ≈ μ0M/B
Curie's law: χ∝1/T, so (∂χ/∂T)_B<0
Maxwell relation (∂S/∂B)_T=(∂m/∂T)_B≈(VB/μ0)(∂χ/∂T)_B shows heat is emitted on isothermal magnetization, ΔQ<0 (Example 17.4)
(∂T/∂B)_S=−(TVB/μ0CB)(∂χ/∂T)_B>0, so adiabatic demagnetization cools a paramagnetic sample — the basis of magnetic refrigeration (Example 17.4)

Microscopic picture: N independent J=1/2 moments give Ω=2^N (S=NkB ln2) when disordered at high T, and Ω=1 (S=0) when fully aligned at very low T; the entropy interpolates between these as kBT is tuned relative to the moment-field energy

The two-step magnetic-cooling cycle: isothermal magnetization (heat expelled to a helium bath) followed by adiabatic demagnetization (thermally isolated, entropy constant, temperature drops); limited in practice by residual internal fields between moments
Show (∂CL/∂L)_T=−T(∂²f/∂T²)_L for an elastic rod (Ex.17.1)
Show (∂T/∂L)_S=−TAETαf/CL for an elastic rod, and use it to explain why a released rubber band under tension feels cooler (Ex.17.2)
Model a rubber molecule as a 1D chain of N=N++N− links; derive L=a(N+−N−), Ω(L)=N!/(N+!N−!), and S≈NkB[ln2−L²/2N²a²], showing S decreases as L increases (Ex.17.3)
Derive dU=CA dT+[γ−T(∂γ/∂T)_A]dA for a liquid surface (Ex.17.4)
Estimate the surface-tension energy per molecule of water in eV and compare it with the molar latent heat per molecule (Ex.17.5)
For a rubber band with f∝T at constant L, show U depends only on T, that adiabatic stretching heats it, and that it contracts on heating at constant tension (Ex.17.6)
Find the work needed to expand a soap bubble from R1 to R2 by driving in a piston, combining isothermal gas compression, surface-energy, and atmospheric-work terms (Ex.17.7)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Different statements of the third law
learningPoints.description: Entropy can only be measured as a difference, S(T)=S(T0)+∫(Cp/T)dT, from heat-capacity data — an absolute value requires fixing S at one reference point

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Different statements of the third law
learningPoints.description: Nernst's statement of the third law: near absolute zero, reactions in a system in internal equilibrium take place with no change in entropy (motivated by ΔG→ΔH as T→0)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Different statements of the third law
learningPoints.description: Planck's statement of the third law: the entropy of any system in internal equilibrium is the same (taken as zero) at absolute zero — equivalent to a non-degenerate (Ω=1) ground state

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Different statements of the third law
learningPoints.description: The apparent paradox of nuclear-spin degeneracy surviving to T=0 is resolved by weak spin–spin interactions lifting the degeneracy via collective excitations (nuclear spin waves), given sufficient cooling

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Different statements of the third law
learningPoints.description: Simon's statement of the third law: each weakly-coupled "aspect" of a system (electrons, nuclear spins, phonons, etc.) has its entropy contribution tend to zero as T→0, though possibly at very different temperatures for each aspect
Heat capacities C=∂S/∂lnT must tend to zero as T→0, since S→0 while lnT→−∞ — this contradicts the classical equipartition prediction of a temperature-independent C
Thermal expansivity βp→0 as T→0, via the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂p)_T→0 implying (∂V/∂T)_p→0
The ideal gas model must break down as T→0: Cp−CV=R cannot hold if both tend to zero, and S=CV lnT+R lnV+constant diverges to −∞, violating the third law
Curie's law (χ∝1/T) must break down as T→0, since (∂S/∂B)_T→0 forces (∂χ/∂T)_B→0 — interactions between moments become unavoidable at low temperature
Unattainability of absolute zero: it is impossible to reach T=0 in a finite number of isothermal-magnetization/adiabatic-demagnetization steps, if the third law holds

A Carnot engine with Tl→0 would approach 100% efficiency, seemingly linking the third law to the second, but an isothermal process exactly at T=0 is physically ill-defined, so the third law is generally treated as an independent postulate
Summarize the main consequences of the third law and how it undermines classical thermodynamic models such as the ideal gas and Curie's law (Ex.18.1)
From H=G−T(∂G/∂T)_p, derive ΔG−ΔH=T(∂ΔG/∂T)_p and discuss what happens to these terms as T→0 (Ex.18.2)
For a system with energy E=αx² in contact with a heat bath, weighting by the Boltzmann factor e^(−βαx²) and normalizing gives ⟨E⟩=(1/2)kBT, independent of α
Generalizing to E=Σαᵢxᵢ² (n independent quadratic modes), the cross terms cancel in the multi-dimensional average, giving ⟨E⟩=(n/2)kBT (Example 19.1)
The equipartition theorem: each independent quadratic energy mode of a classical system in contact with a heat reservoir at T contributes mean energy (1/2)kBT
A mass-on-a-spring's mean thermal energy kBT≈0.025eV at room temperature applies equally to a macroscopic spring and to an atom on a chemical bond (Example 19.2)
Translational motion in a monatomic gas: 3 quadratic modes give ⟨E⟩=(3/2)kBT, matching the earlier kinetic-theory result
Rotational motion in a diatomic gas adds 2 modes (about the two axes perpendicular to the bond; the third axis has negligible moment of inertia and is frozen out), giving ⟨E⟩=(5/2)kBT
Vibrational motion of the bond (modelled as a spring with reduced mass μ) adds 2 more modes, giving ⟨E⟩=(7/2)kBT if fully excited
From ⟨E⟩=(f/2)kBT: CV=(f/2)R and Cp=(f/2+1)R per mole, so γ=1+2/f, tabulated for monatomic and diatomic gases with/without vibration
Heat capacity of a solid: modelling each atom as connected by springs to 6 neighbours (3N springs for N atoms, each with 2 quadratic modes) gives ⟨E⟩=3NkBT and CV=3R per mole — the Dulong–Petit rule
Equipartition assumes a mode's variable ranges continuously; it fails at low temperature, where kBT is smaller than the quantum energy-level spacing ℏω — equipartition is a high-temperature theory

Taylor-expanding a smooth potential well about its minimum shows it is approximately quadratic there (the harmonic approximation), justifying equipartition — though this breaks down if T is high enough to probe the well's anharmonic terms

Brownian motion: equipartition gives a pollen grain's translational kinetic energy (3/2)kBT regardless of mass, so lighter grains show more pronounced thermal jiggling, resisted by viscous damping (Example 19.3)
Find the mean kinetic energy in eV of various noble-gas atoms at room temperature (Ex.19.1)
Interpret measured molar Cp values (in units of R) for various solids and gases against the Dulong–Petit and diatomic-gas equipartition predictions (Ex.19.2)
Show a potential V(r)=A/r^n−B/r is approximately quadratic near its minimum, and find the mean thermal energy there (Ex.19.3)
Derive ⟨xᵢ²⟩=kBT/2αᵢ from the n-quadratic-mode setup of Example 19.1 (Ex.19.4)
Show ⟨E⟩=kBT for a non-quadratic energy E=α|x| (Ex.19.5)
Show ⟨E⟩=ξkBT for E=α|x|ⁿ, for general n (Ex.19.6)
Derive the mean-square angular amplitude ⟨θ²⟩ of a simple pendulum in thermal equilibrium at temperature T (Ex.19.7)
Single-particle partition function Z=Σ_α e^(−βEα), a sum of Boltzmann factors over all states of the system
The zero of energy (and hence Z) is arbitrary up to a multiplicative constant; quantities built from lnZ are defined up to an additive constant, but differentials of lnZ are determined precisely
Partition function of a two-level system (energies ±Δ/2): Z=2cosh(βΔ/2) (Example 20.1)
Partition function of the simple harmonic oscillator (energies (n+1/2)ℏω): Z=e^(−βℏω/2)/(1−e^(−βℏω)) (Example 20.1)
Partition function of an N equally-spaced-level system (finite geometric sum) and of a diatomic molecule's rotational levels, with (2J+1)-fold degeneracy (Example 20.2)
U=−dlnZ/dβ=kBT²(dlnZ/dT), by recognizing ΣEᵢe^(−βEᵢ) as −dZ/dβ
S=U/T+kB lnZ, from lnPj=−βEj−lnZ substituted into the Gibbs entropy formula
F=−kBT lnZ (equivalently Z=e^(−βF)), from F=U−TS
Once F(T,V) is known from Z, standard thermodynamic derivatives give S, p, H, G, and CV — in practice only the U and F formulas need to be remembered

Two-level system: U, CV, F, S worked out from Z=2cosh(βΔ/2); entropy runs from 0 (only the ground state occupied) to kB ln2 (both states equally likely); CV shows a broad Schottky-anomaly peak around T~Δ/kB (Example 20.3)
Simple harmonic oscillator: U, CV, F, S worked out from Z; the high-T limit recovers the equipartition result CV→kB, while CV→0 and S→0 as T→0 (Example 20.3)
At high temperature, the rotational partition function's sum can be approximated by an integral, giving Z≈1/(βΔ) and hence CV=kB, recovering the equipartition result for a rotating diatomic molecule

The "big idea" of statistical mechanics: describe a system by its energy levels, write down Z, then derive all functions of state from it; qualitative behaviour is set by comparing kBT to the energy-level spacings (frozen out, equally populated, or equipartition-like)
If a system's energy is a sum of independent contributions, its partition function factorizes, Z=Za·Zb (so lnZ=lnZa+lnZb, and state functions built from lnZ simply add)
N independent simple harmonic oscillators have Z=Z_SHO^N; a diatomic molecule's vibrational and rotational partition functions multiply, Z=Zvib·Zrot (Example 20.4)
Spin-1/2 paramagnet: single-particle Z1=2cosh(βμBB) for a two-state spin in a field; N independent spins give Z=Z1^N
Magnetic moment m=NμB tanh(βμBB), from m=−(∂F/∂B)_T; saturates to NμB at low T/high B, vanishes at high T/low B
Small-field expansion tanh(x)≈x gives Curie's law, χ≈Nμ0μB²/(VkBT) (Example 20.5)
Find the high-temperature limits of the SHO and rotational partition functions, Z≈(βℏω)⁻¹ and Z≈(βℏ²/2I)⁻¹, and the resulting U, C, F, S (Ex.20.1)
Show lnPj=β(F−Ej) (Ex.20.2)
Rewrite the simple harmonic oscillator's U and S in coth/sinh form (Ex.20.3)
Show the SHO's zero-point energy contributes to U and F but not to S or CV (Ex.20.4)
Derive U, C, and S for N independent spin-1/2 particles in a magnetic field (Ex.20.5)
For a 4-level magnetic system, find the partition function, Helmholtz function, magnetization, and generalized Curie susceptibility (Ex.20.6)
Find the partition function, Helmholtz function, and high-temperature heat capacity of 3 independent harmonic oscillators (a 3D oscillator) (Ex.20.7)
For a hydrogen atom's internal energy levels, show the partition function sum diverges, then estimate the mean energy at 300K from a truncated 2-level approximation (Ex.20.8)
From U=−m·B and TS=U+F, derive TδS=−B·δm and check consistency with the first law for a paramagnet (Ex.20.9)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Particle-in-a-box wavefunctions vanishing at the walls give discrete allowed wavevectors kx=nxπ/L (and similarly ky,kz), so allowed states form a uniform grid in k-space with volume (π/L)³ per state

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Density of states g(k)dk=Vk²dk/2π², from counting states in one octant of a spherical shell in k-space (equivalently, over a full sphere with periodic boundary conditions, Example 21.1)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Single-particle partition function of an ideal gas, replacing the sum over states with an integral over the density of states, Z1=∫e^(−βE(k))g(k)dk=VnQ, where nQ=(1/ℏ³)(mkBT/2π)^(3/2) is the quantum concentration

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Thermal wavelength λth=nQ^(−1/3)=h/√(2πmkBT), so Z1=V/λth³

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: For N distinguishable particles, ZN=(Z1)^N, illustrated via a 2-particle 2-level toy model (Example 21.2)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: For indistinguishable particles, (Z1)^N overcounts states where multiple particles share an energy level; if such multiple occupancy is rare (n≪nQ), the overcounting factor is just N!, giving ZN=(Z1)^N/N!

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: The validity condition n≪nQ holds well for ordinary gas molecules (e.g. N2 in air) but fails for electrons in a metal, which require proper quantum-degenerate treatment

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Functions of state of the ideal gas
learningPoints.description: lnZN=N lnV+(3N/2)lnT+constants for the N-particle ideal-gas partition function; U=−dlnZN/dβ=(3/2)NkBT and CV=(3/2)NkB, matching earlier results

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Functions of state of the ideal gas
learningPoints.description: p=−(∂F/∂V)_T=NkBT/V recovers the ideal gas law directly from the partition function; H=(5/2)NkBT follows

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Functions of state of the ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Using Stirling's approximation to make the N! explicit, F=NkBT[ln(nλth³)−1], leading to the Sackur–Tetrode entropy S=NkB[5/2−ln(nλth³)]

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Functions of state of the ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Gibbs function G=NkBT ln(nλth³)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: The Sackur–Tetrode entropy applied to a Joule expansion recovers ΔS=NkB ln2, consistent with 1 bit of "which half" uncertainty per molecule

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: The Gibbs paradox: mixing two distinguishable gases gives ΔS=2NkB ln2, but mixing two samples of a truly identical gas must give ΔS=0, since removing the partition is then a reversible, no-information-loss operation

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Gibbs' resolution: permutations of identical particles must count as the same state (the N! in ZN); omitting this division gives a non-extensive entropy expression — the original form of the paradox

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Heat capacity of a diatomic gas
learningPoints.description: A diatomic molecule's partition function factorizes as Z=Ztrans·Zvib·Zrot, so U and CV are each sums of the individual mode contributions

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.sectionTitle: Heat capacity of a diatomic gas
learningPoints.description: The resulting CV(T) rises through a series of plateaus (3/2R → 5/2R → 7/2R) as translational, then rotational (T≳ℏ²/2IkB), then vibrational (T≳ℏω/kB) modes activate — matching the equipartition high-T limit while showing the low-T freezing-out that equipartition alone misses

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Show the single-particle partition function of a 2D gas confined to area A is Z1=A/λth² (Ex.21.1)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Show the Sackur–Tetrode entropy is extensive, but that omitting the N! (the "distinguishable-particle" entropy) is not — the original form of the Gibbs paradox (Ex.21.2)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Find the number of states below Emax, and show it equals ΞVnQ for Emax~(3/2)kBT (Ex.21.3)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: For a two-level atom combined with translational motion, find the atomic partition function, its Schottky-like heat capacity, and the gas's total heat capacity (Ex.21.4)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Explain the measured heat capacity curve of H2 gas as a function of temperature (Ex.21.5)

learningPoints.chapterTitle: Statistical mechanics of an ideal gas
learningPoints.description: Find the single-particle partition function of a gas of hydrogen atoms including their internal ground-state binding energy, Z1=Ve^(βR)/λth³ (Ex.21.6)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: A definition of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: Adding particles modifies the first law to dU=TdS−pdV+μdN, giving the chemical potential μ=(∂U/∂N)_(S,V)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: A definition of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: More experimentally convenient definitions of μ from F and G: μ=(∂F/∂N)_(V,T) and μ=(∂G/∂N)_(p,T)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The meaning of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: Writing S=S(U,V,N) and comparing with dS from the first law identifies (∂S/∂U)_(N,V)=1/T, (∂S/∂V)_(N,U)=p/T, (∂S/∂N)_(U,V)=−μ/T

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The meaning of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: For two systems exchanging only heat, maximizing total entropy (dS≥0) shows heat flows from hot to cold and equilibrium requires T1=T2

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The meaning of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: For two systems exchanging only particles, the analogous entropy-maximization argument shows particles flow from higher to lower chemical potential, with equilibrium at μ1=μ2 — μ plays the role for particle flow that 1/T plays for heat flow

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The meaning of the chemical potential
learningPoints.description: Chemical potential of an ideal gas, μ=kBT ln(nλth³), derived from F=NkBT[ln(nλth³)−1] (Example 22.1)
Taylor-expanding a reservoir's entropy for a small energy/particle exchange (ε,N) with a small system gives the Gibbs distribution P(ε,N)∝e^(β(μN−ε))
Grand partition function Ξ=Σᵢe^(β(μNᵢ−Eᵢ)); the grand canonical ensemble reduces to the canonical (Boltzmann) distribution when μ=0
Expressions for N, U, and S in terms of the grand partition function Ξ and its derivatives
Comparing the three ensembles: microcanonical (fixed U, Ω=e^(βTS)), canonical (fixed T, Z=e^(−βF)), and grand canonical (fixed T and μ, Ξ=e^(−βΦG))
Grand potential ΦG=−kBT lnΞ=U−TS−μN=F−μN
dΦG=−SdT−pdV−Ndμ, giving S=−(∂ΦG/∂T)_(V,μ), p=−(∂ΦG/∂V)_(T,μ), N=−(∂ΦG/∂μ)_(T,V)
Grand potential of an ideal gas, ΦG=−NkBT=−pV, verified to give the correct p and N via its partial derivatives (Example 22.2)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Chemical potential as Gibbs function per particle
learningPoints.description: Using the extensivity of S(U,V,N), U−TS+pV=μN, so G=μN and μ=G/N — the chemical potential is the Gibbs function per particle

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Chemical potential as Gibbs function per particle
learningPoints.description: This extensivity argument also shows that the grand potential ΦG=−pV always holds, not just for the ideal gas
With multiple particle species, dU=TdS−pdV+Σμᵢ dNᵢ; at fixed T,p this gives dG=Σμᵢ dNᵢ
If particle number isn't conserved, equilibrium requires minimizing F freely with respect to N, giving μ=0 — true for photons (in vacuum)
For electron–positron pair production/annihilation (e⁻+e⁺⇌γ), minimizing F subject to fixed N=N⁺−N⁻ shows μ⁺+μ⁻=0
Pressure dependence of an ideal gas's chemical potential, μ(p)=μ°+kBT ln(p/p°) (Example 22.3)
For a simple reaction A⇌B, the equilibrium constant K=pB/pA; setting ΔrG=ΔrG°+RT ln(pB/pA)=0 at equilibrium gives lnK=−ΔrG°/RT
Generalizing to a multi-species reaction, equilibrium requires Σνⱼμⱼ=0 (Examples 22.4–22.5), and the equilibrium constant K=Π(pⱼ/p°)^νⱼ satisfies the same lnK=−ΔrG°/RT relation (Example 22.6)

The van't Hoff equation, d(lnK)/d(1/T)=−ΔrH°/R, from combining lnK=−ΔrG°/RT with the Gibbs–Helmholtz relation; consistent with Le Chatelier's principle (K falls with T for exothermic reactions, rises for endothermic ones)
H2→H·+H· dissociation equilibrium constant vs. T yields a bond enthalpy ~440 kJ/mol (~4.5 eV) via a van't Hoff plot (Example 22.7)

Osmosis: a semipermeable membrane passes solvent but not solute; osmotic flow raises the solution's level until the osmotic pressure Π balances it — an entropic force, like the tension of stretched rubber
Chemical potential of a solvent in a dilute ideal solution, μA(liquid)=μA*(pure liquid)+RT ln(xA), using Raoult's law pA=xA pA* (Example 22.8)
Equilibrium between pure solvent at pressure p and solution at p+Π gives ΠVA=−RT ln xA≈RTxB for a dilute solution, i.e. the van't Hoff osmotic-pressure law ΠV=nBRT

Microscopic picture of osmotic flow: asymmetric momentum transfer near the membrane's pores (solute molecules are only "kicked" one way) drags solvent through, resisted only by an applied osmotic pressure; real-world examples include plant turgor pressure and reverse-osmosis desalination
Maximize the Gibbs entropy subject to ΣPi=1, ΣPiEi=U, ΣPiNi=N to re-derive the grand canonical (Gibbs) distribution (Ex.22.1)
Show the fugacity z=e^(βμ)=nλth³ for an ideal gas, and interpret the z≪1 and z≫1 limits (Ex.22.2)
Estimate the bond enthalpy of Br2 from a van't Hoff plot of its dissociation equilibrium constant (Ex.22.3)
Derive the grand-partition-function expressions for N, U, and S (Ex.22.4)
Derive μ=−kBT ln(Z1/N) for indistinguishable particles from ZN=Z1^N/N! (Ex.22.5)

Derive the Saha equation for hydrogen ionization equilibrium (H⇌p⁺+e⁻) from chemical-potential balance and the hydrogen partition function; derive the degree-of-ionization formula and explain why lower density favors more ionization (Ex.22.6)
Show the osmotic pressure of blood (~0.9% NaCl solution) is about 8× atmospheric pressure (Ex.22.7)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The classical thermodynamics of electromagnetic radiation
learningPoints.description: Photons have energy ℏω and momentum ℏk, with ω/k=c

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The classical thermodynamics of electromagnetic radiation
learningPoints.description: For a photon gas, radiation pressure p=u/3 (u=energy density), differing from the kinetic-theory factor 2u/3 for a non-relativistic gas because photon energy is written as mc² rather than (1/2)m⟨v²⟩

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The classical thermodynamics of electromagnetic radiation
learningPoints.description: Photon flux on a cavity wall Φ=(1/4)nc and incident power per unit area F=(1/4)uc, by analogy with the kinetic-theory flux results

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The classical thermodynamics of electromagnetic radiation
learningPoints.description: Combining dU=TdS−pdV with p=u/3 and a Maxwell relation gives 4u=T(∂u/∂T)_V, integrating to the Stefan–Boltzmann law u=AT⁴ and F=σT⁴
Spectral energy density uλ (or uν), with u=∫uλdλ

Comparing two cavities of different material/shape joined by a filtered tube, the second law (no net heat flow between equal-T reservoirs) shows the spectral energy density is a universal function of λ,T only, independent of the cavity's material or shape
Spectral absorptivity αλ and spectral emissive power eλ
Kirchhoff's law, eλ/αλ=(c/4)uλ, a universal function of λ,T — "good absorbers are good emitters" at the same wavelength (Example 23.1)
A perfect black body has αλ=1 for all λ, making it the best possible emitter; a black-body cavity contains black-body radiation
Modelling the Sun and Earth as black bodies gives TEarth/TSun=√(RSun/2D) (Example 23.2)
For isotropic black-body radiation, p=u/3, giving F=σT⁴, u=(4σ/c)T⁴, p=4σT⁴/3c
For a collimated beam (all photons travelling one way), the radiation pressure is instead p=u=σT⁴/c, from the momentum ℏk absorbed per unit time per unit area
Sunlight's radiation pressure on Earth (~4.6μPa) is about ten orders of magnitude below atmospheric pressure (Example 23.3)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The statistical mechanics of the photon gas
learningPoints.description: Photon dispersion ω=ck gives a density of states g(ω)dω=Vω²dω/π²c³, analogous to the ideal-gas calculation but with a factor of 2 for polarization

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The statistical mechanics of the photon gas
learningPoints.description: Treating each mode as an independent SHO, U=∫g(ω)ℏω[1/2+1/(e^(βℏω)−1)]dω; the zero-point sum diverges and is discarded by redefining the energy zero

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The statistical mechanics of the photon gas
learningPoints.description: Evaluating the remaining integral (via x=ℏβω) gives U∝VT⁴, establishing the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ=π²kB⁴/60c²ℏ³ from first principles
The black-body spectral energy density (Planck's law), uω=(ℏ/π²c³)ω³/(e^(βℏω)−1), and its ν, λ forms

The low-frequency (hν≪kBT) limit recovers the classical Rayleigh–Jeans law, uν→8πkBTν²/c³; integrating this form over all frequencies diverges (the ultraviolet catastrophe), resolved by the full quantum black-body form
Wien's displacement law, λmaxT=constant, from setting duλ/dλ=0; the room-temperature black-body peak lies in the infrared (~10μm)
The uν and uλ maxima occur at different λT products (5.1 vs. 2.9 mm·K) because they are densities per unit frequency vs. per unit wavelength
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is isotropic (to ~1 part in 10⁵) black-body radiation at 2.7K, discovered by Penzias and Wilson — key evidence for the hot big bang

As the Universe expands, radiation energy density falls as T⁴ (Stefan–Boltzmann) while also diluting geometrically, so temperature is inversely proportional to the scale factor — the Universe was hotter and denser in the past

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The Einstein A and B coefficients
learningPoints.description: The Einstein A and B coefficients model spontaneous emission (rate A21N2), absorption (rate B12N1uω), and stimulated emission (rate B21N2uω) for a two-level atomic system in a radiation field

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The Einstein A and B coefficients
learningPoints.description: Balancing these three rates in steady state, and requiring Boltzmann-factor level populations in thermal equilibrium, recovers the black-body spectral form and gives the Einstein relations B21/B12=g1/g2 and A21=(ℏω³/π²c³)B21

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The Einstein A and B coefficients
learningPoints.description: Laser gain requires a population inversion (N2/g2>N1/g1), which cannot occur in a simple two-level system in thermal equilibrium — hence real lasers need extra levels to pump the upper level and drain the lower one (Example 23.4)
Find the Earth–Sun temperature ratio including Earth's albedo A (Ex.23.1)
Derive the Wien's-law transcendental equation x=α(1−e^(−x)) and solve it iteratively for the uν and uλ maxima (Ex.23.2)
Find the CMB photon energy density, the photon flux/energy landing on an outstretched hand, and the radiation pressure felt from the CMB (Ex.23.3)
Find the ratio of solar to CMB photon flux on an outstretched hand (Ex.23.4)
Derive the thermodynamic identities for a photon gas — entropy density s=4p/T, G=0, Cv=3s, and interpret the "infinite Cp" result (Ex.23.5)
Derive the photon-gas partition function lnZ=Vπ²(kBT)³/45ℏ³c³ by integration by parts, then F, S, U, p, and the relations U=−3F, pV=U/3, S=4U/3T (Ex.23.6)
Find the total photon number N in black-body radiation, the mean energy per photon (2.701kBT), and the mean entropy per photon, compared with the classical ideal-gas values (Ex.23.7)
The Einstein model assumes all 3N vibrational modes of a solid share one frequency ωE; since modes are independent, Z=(Z_SHO)^(3N)
Molar internal energy U=3RΘE[1/2+1/(e^(ΘE/T)−1)], where ΘE=ℏωE/kB is the Einstein temperature; U→3RT at high T
Molar heat capacity C=3R x²eˣ/(eˣ−1)² (x=ΘE/T); C→3R (Dulong–Petit) as T→∞, and C→3Rx²e^(−x)→0 exponentially as T→0 (Example 24.1)
The Debye model improves on Einstein's single-frequency assumption with a continuous spectrum of modes, ω=vsq (sound waves), up to a maximum (Debye) frequency ωD fixed by requiring ∫g(ω)dω=3N
Density of states g(ω)dω=3Vω²dω/2π²vs³ (three polarizations) before truncation, giving g(ω)dω=9Nω²dω/ωD³ after imposing the 3N-mode normalization; ΘD=ℏωD/kB defines the Debye temperature
Internal energy U=(9/8)NℏωD+(9Nℏ/ωD³)∫₀^ωD ω³dω/(e^(βℏω)−1), from integrating the SHO energy over the Debye density of states (Example 24.2)
At high temperature, C→3R (Dulong–Petit, matching equipartition); at low temperature, C→3R(4π⁴/5)(T/ΘD)³ — the Debye T³ law (Example 24.3)
For a monatomic linear chain of masses/springs, the exact dispersion relation is ω=√(4K/m)|sin(qa/2)|, reducing to the linear ω=vsq (vs=a√(K/m)) only in the long-wavelength limit qa→0

Real 3D solids (e.g. Cu) show this linear-at-small-q behaviour experimentally (via inelastic neutron scattering), justifying the Debye approximation at low temperature, where only long-wavelength phonons are thermally excited

A diatomic chain's dispersion splits into an acoustic branch (ω→0 as q→0, atoms in phase, like ordinary sound) and an optic branch (ω finite at q=0, atoms out of phase, can couple to EM radiation if the atoms are charged) — the acoustic branch is well described by the Debye model, the optic branch by the Einstein model
Estimate the maximum phonon frequency and speed of sound from a given lattice parameter and Debye temperature (Ex.24.1)
Rewrite the Debye internal-energy formula via the substitution x=ℏβω (Ex.24.2)
Show the Debye model in d dimensions predicts a low-temperature heat capacity ∝T^d (Ex.24.3)
Derive the density of states for a monatomic linear chain, g(ω)=(2L/πa)[4K/m−ω²]^(−1/2), and discuss its singularity (Ex.24.4)
Generalize the monatomic-chain dispersion to a 2D square lattice, and find the speed of sound (Ex.24.5)
Derive the two-branch dispersion relation for a diatomic chain (Ex.24.6)
Generalize the monatomic chain to include further-neighbour force constants, derive the resulting dispersion relation and its Fourier-inversion formula for the force constants (Ex.24.7)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Relativistic dispersion relation for massive particles
learningPoints.description: Relativistic dispersion relation E²=p²c²+m²c⁴; reduces to E=p²/2m+mc² (non-relativistic, p≪mc) or E=pc (ultrarelativistic, p≫mc)
Single-particle partition function for an ultrarelativistic gas, Z1=∫e^(−βℏkc)g(k)dk=V(kBT/ℏc)³/π², using the same density of states as the non-relativistic ideal gas but with E=ℏkc
Z1∝VT³ for the ultrarelativistic gas vs. VT^(3/2) for the non-relativistic gas; Z1=V/Λ³ defines a relativistic analogue of the thermal wavelength
From lnZN=N lnV+3N lnT+const, U=3NkBT and CV=3NkB — different from the non-relativistic (3/2)NkBT, because equipartition (which assumes a quadratic dispersion) fails for the linear E=pc relation
p=NkBT/V (still the ideal gas law, since Z1∝V in both cases) and H=4NkBT; after Stirling's approximation, F, S, and G follow in terms of nΛ³ (Example 25.1)
p=u/3 for the ultrarelativistic gas (vs. p=2u/3 non-relativistically), with consequences for stellar structure

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ultrarelativistic gas
learningPoints.description: Adiabatic (constant-entropy) expansion of an ultrarelativistic gas keeps nΛ³ constant, giving VT³=constant and pV^(4/3)=constant, i.e. γ=4/3 (vs. γ=5/3 non-relativistically)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ultrarelativistic gas
learningPoints.description: Applied to the expanding Universe: CMB photons cool as T∝a⁻¹ (ultrarelativistic) vs. non-relativistic matter cooling as T∝a⁻² (Example 25.2)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Adiabatic expansion of an ultrarelativistic gas
learningPoints.description: Density scales as ρ∝a⁻³ for non-relativistic matter but ρ∝a⁻⁴ for relativistic species (an extra factor from energy redshift), so the early Universe was radiation-dominated while today it is matter-dominated
Find the phase and group velocity for a relativistic particle, and their non-relativistic/ultrarelativistic limits (Ex.25.1)
Derive the density of states in D dimensions with spin degeneracy g (Ex.25.2)

For a general dispersion relation E=αp^s, derive the density of states g(E) and the single-particle partition function Z1=V/λ^D, and check it reduces to the non-relativistic (s=2) and ultrarelativistic (s=1) 3D cases (Ex.25.3)
Van der Waals equation of state, (p+a/Vm²)(Vm−b)=RT, with a=intermolecular attraction strength, b=excluded volume

Motivation for the a/Vm² term: attractive interactions lower the energy by an amount ∝nmoles²/V, giving an effective pressure correction; equivalently derived statistically by shrinking the available volume to V−nmolesb and including a Boltzmann factor e^(βan²/V)
Van der Waals isotherms become S-shaped below a critical temperature, giving a region of negative (unstable) compressibility κT
Critical point (Tc,pc,Vc) found from ∂p/∂V=∂²p/∂V²=0, giving Vc=3b, Tc=8a/27Rb, pc=a/27b², and the universal ratio pcVc/RTc=3/8 (Example 26.1)

Below Tc, the Gibbs function becomes multiply-valued vs. pressure; the system follows the lower branch, giving phase coexistence (liquid/gas) where G is equal at two volumes, with metastable superheated-liquid/supercooled-gas branches in between
The Maxwell construction: the phase-coexistence pressure is set by requiring ∫V dp=0 between the two coexisting volumes (equal-area construction)

Van der Waals pressure splits into a repulsive hard-sphere term RT/(V−b) and an attractive term −a/V²; alternative models make the attractive term temperature-dependent (Berthelot) or exponential (Dieterici)
Dieterici equation of state, p(Vm−b)=RT e^(−a/RTVm)
Dieterici critical point Tc=a/4Rb, pc=a/4e²b², Vc=2b, giving pcVc/RTc=2/e²≈0.271 — closer to real noble-gas data than the van der Waals value of 0.375
Virial expansion, pVm/RT=1+B/Vm+C/Vm²+...; the Boyle temperature TB is where B(T)=0
Expanding the van der Waals equation in 1/V gives B(T)=b−a/RT, and TB=a/bR=27Tc/8 (Example 26.2)

Statistical-mechanical derivation of the second virial coefficient from the intermolecular pair potential, B(T)=(N/2)∫d³r[1−e^(−βV(r))], via factorizing Z into kinetic and potential-energy parts under a dilute-gas pairwise-collision approximation

B(T) is large and negative at low T (dominated by the attractive potential well) and small and positive at high T (dominated by the short-range repulsive core) — explaining the sign change at the Boyle temperature

The law of corresponding states: reduced coordinates p̃=p/pc, Ṽ=V/Vc, T̃=T/Tc collapse different substances' equations of state onto a common form, since intermolecular potentials share the same qualitative shape (repulsive core + attractive well), differing only in length/energy scale
The reduced van der Waals equation of state, (p̃+3/Ṽ²)=8T̃/(3Ṽ−1) (Example 26.3), and real liquid–gas coexistence curves for different substances collapsing onto one curve in reduced coordinates
Show the isothermal compressibility of a van der Waals gas at V=Vc diverges as κT∝(T−Tc)⁻¹, and discuss what happens on cooling through Tc (Ex.26.1)
For the equation of state p(V−b)=RT, estimate the order of magnitude of b and show U depends only on T (Ex.26.2)
Express the Dieterici equation of state in reduced variables (Ex.26.3)
Derive the isobaric expansivity βp of a van der Waals gas, and describe its behaviour near the critical point (Ex.26.4)
Derive U=(3/2)RT−a/V for one mole of van der Waals gas from the statistical-mechanical partition function (Ex.26.5)
For a van der Waals gas with U=(f/2)RT−a/V, show CV=(f/2)R and Cp−CV≈R+2a/TV (Ex.26.6)
Joule coefficient μJ=(∂T/∂V)_U
μJ=−(1/CV)(∂U/∂V)_T=−(1/CV)[T(∂p/∂T)_V−p], using a Maxwell relation and the first law
μJ=0 for an ideal gas; real gases cool in a Joule expansion (μJ<0) because increasing intermolecular separation raises the (negative) potential energy, forcing kinetic energy (and T) down at fixed U
Joule coefficient of a van der Waals gas, μJ=−a/(CV V²) (Example 27.1); integrating gives ΔT=−(a/CV)(1/V1−1/V2)<0 for an expansion (Example 27.2)
Change in U during isothermal expansion, ΔU=∫[T(∂p/∂T)_V−p]dV; zero for an ideal gas, but ΔU=a(1/V1−1/V2) for a van der Waals gas — U depends on a (attraction) but not b (excluded volume)
Entropy of a van der Waals gas, S=CV lnT+R ln(V−b)+constant — S depends on b but not a, since entropy only cares about available configuration space (Example 27.3)
In a steady-flow throttling process, the work done pushing gas through (p1V1 in, p2V2 out) means enthalpy H=U+pV is conserved, not U
Joule–Kelvin coefficient μJK=(∂T/∂p)_H
μJK=(1/Cp)[T(∂V/∂T)_p−V], using dH=TdS+Vdp and a Maxwell relation

μJK can be positive or negative; the inversion curve (∂V/∂T)_p=V/T marks where it changes sign; the maximum inversion temperature sets the ceiling below which Joule–Kelvin cooling is possible (varies hugely by gas)
A practical liquefier uses a counter-current heat exchanger to precool the incoming gas with the outgoing cold exhaust, so the gas reaches the throttle valve below its inversion temperature
Liquefier efficiency y (mass fraction liquefied) from enthalpy conservation, y=(hf−hi)/(hf−hL); maximizing y over the incoming pressure requires μJK=0, i.e. operating exactly on the inversion curve
Historical liquefaction milestones — Linde's counter-current process, Dewar's liquid/solid hydrogen, Kamerlingh Onnes's liquid helium and the subsequent discovery of superconductivity
Derive the general relations (∂T/∂V)_U, (∂T/∂V)_S, (∂T/∂p)_H, identify which expansion each governs, and verify their ideal-gas limits (Ex.27.1)
Explain enthalpy conservation in Joule–Kelvin throttling, and estimate helium's maximum starting temperature for cooling using its virial-expansion Boyle temperature (Ex.27.2)
Derive the inversion curve of a Dieterici gas and its maximum inversion temperature (Ex.27.3)
Express the Dieterici inversion curve in reduced units (Ex.27.4)
Use tabulated enthalpy-vs-pressure data for helium at 14K to find the input pressure that maximizes the liquefied fraction α (Ex.27.5)
Latent heat L=Tc(S2−S1), the extra reversible heat needed to convert phase 1 to phase 2 at the transition temperature; produces a spike in Cx=T(∂S/∂T)_x
Kettle-boiling-dry time estimate, comparing sensible heat (warming) to latent heat (vaporizing) (Example 28.1)
Rough microscopic estimate of the vapour–liquid entropy jump from the ratio of accessible volumes, ΔS≈R ln(ρliq/ρvap)≈7R, giving Trouton's rule L≈7–10RTb
Trouton's rule holds well (L/RTb≈8–10) for many substances via the law of corresponding states, but fails for helium (quantum effects) and water (polar, hydrogen-bonded)

For two phases in equilibrium at constant T,p, minimizing the total Gibbs function (dGtot=0, dN1=−dN2) gives μ1=μ2 — coexisting phases share the same chemical potential, and the lowest-μ phase is stable
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation, dp/dT=L/[T(V2−V1)], from requiring dμ1=dμ2 along the phase boundary and using dμ=−s dT+v dp
Assuming L constant, an ideal vapour, and Vvapour≫Vliquid gives the exponential vapour-pressure curve p=p0 exp(−L/RT) (Example 28.2)
Accounting for L's temperature dependence via Cpv−CpL gives L=L0+(Cpv−CpL)T and a modified phase-boundary equation (Example 28.3)
For the liquid–solid boundary, neglecting L and ΔV's temperature dependence gives a linear p(T) relation (steep, since ΔV is small) (Example 28.4)
A full p–T phase diagram has solid/liquid/gas regions meeting at a triple point; the liquid–gas boundary terminates at a critical point but the solid–liquid boundary does not

Water's solid–liquid coexistence line has an anomalous negative slope (ice is less dense than water, from hydrogen bonding), with wide-ranging consequences (icebergs float, lakes freeze from the top, glacier flow)
(∂μ/∂p)_T=v>0 and (∂μ/∂T)_p=−s<0 mean the higher-pressure stable phase has the smaller volume, and the higher-temperature stable phase has the higher entropy
Crossing a phase boundary, the system can persist metastably on the "wrong" branch (superheated liquid, supercooled vapour) if nucleation of the new phase is kinetically hindered

Kelvin's formula: extra pressure Δp=2γ/r inside a curved liquid surface shifts the equilibrium vapour pressure, p=p0 exp(2γVliq/rRT); small droplets have anomalously high vapour pressure (evaporate rather than grow), stabilizing supercooled vapour until nucleated on dust or other surfaces
Superheated liquids similarly resist bubble formation, since small vapour cavities have depressed internal pressure and tend to collapse — the basis of bumping and of bubble chambers (Example 28.5)

Gibbs function of a growing liquid droplet, G(r)=G(0)+4πγr²−(4π/3)Δμ(ρliq/m)r³, has a maximum (not minimum) at a critical radius r*=2γm/(ρliqΔμ) — an unstable equilibrium separating shrinking from growing droplets (Example 28.6)
Mole fraction xi=ni/n, Σxi=1; components (chemically independent constituents) vs. phases
The Gibbs phase rule, F=C−P+2, from counting intensive variables (2+P(C−1)) against the equilibrium constraints (C(P−1)) between P coexisting phases of C components
For a single-component system, F=3−P: one phase spans the p–T plane, two phases coexist along a line, three phases (triple point) coexist only at a point (Example 28.7)
Dissolving a solute lowers the solvent's chemical potential, elevating its boiling point and depressing its freezing point — colligative properties

Boiling-point elevation T−T*≈RT*²xB/ΔHvap=KbxB (ebullioscopic constant), from the vapour–liquid equilibrium condition and a dilute-solution expansion; an analogous freezing-point depression T*−T=KfxB (cryoscopic constant) follows the same route
Physically, dissolved solute raises the solvent's entropy, weakening its thermodynamic drive to change phase — hence both effects (e.g. salted roads, ocean freezing point)

Ehrenfest's classification: the order of a phase transition is the order of the lowest derivative of G that is discontinuous at Tc; first-order transitions have discontinuous S,V (a latent heat); "second-order" transitions have continuous S,V but discontinuous/divergent Cp,κT

The modern classification instead distinguishes first-order (has latent heat) from continuous (no latent heat) transitions — motivated by the breakdown of mean thermodynamic quantities from large fluctuations near a critical point (Example 28.8)

Symmetry breaking: a solid has less symmetry than the liquid it froze from, and this loss of symmetry cannot happen gradually, so symmetry-breaking transitions are always sharp and lack a critical point (unlike the liquid–gas line)

Not all transitions involve symmetry breaking — the liquid–gas transition can be avoided entirely by routing around the critical point, since liquid and gas share the same symmetry, differing only in density; symmetry-breaking is a very general concept, extending to the electroweak phase transition in the early Universe

The Ising model: a lattice of spins Si=±1 with Hamiltonian H=−JΣ⟨i,j⟩SiSj (J>0 ferromagnetic, J<0 antiferromagnetic); minimizing energy favors all-aligned states, but minimizing F=U−TS favors disorder at high T since disordered microstates vastly outnumber ordered ones

Four Ising spins on a square: Z=12+cosh(4βJ), giving ⟨E⟩ that smoothly interpolates between −4J (T→0) and 0 (T→∞); illustrates that sharp phase transitions only emerge in the large-system limit, though the ground-state degeneracy (m=±4) persists at any size (Example 28.9)

In 1D, inserting a domain wall costs finite energy (2J) but gains unbounded entropy (kB lnN) as N→∞, so ΔF<0 for any T>0 — no long-range order survives in 1D at any nonzero temperature; in 2D and higher a single defect can't destroy long-range order this way, and the 2D Ising model does have a genuine phase transition (solved exactly by Onsager)
The number of Ising configurations (2^(N²) for an N×N lattice) grows too fast to enumerate exactly for large systems, motivating Monte Carlo methods

Fluctuation-response relations from the partition function: C=kBβ²(⟨E²⟩−⟨E⟩²) relates heat capacity to energy fluctuations, and ⟨X²⟩−⟨X⟩²=kBTχ relates a generalized susceptibility to fluctuations in its conjugate variable

The Metropolis Monte Carlo algorithm (randomly flip a spin; always accept if it lowers energy, otherwise accept with probability e^(−βΔE)) drives the system toward its Boltzmann-weighted equilibrium ensemble; near Tc the correlation length diverges, causing critical slowing down in both real systems and simulations
Estimate lead's melting-point shift at 100 atm using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation (Ex.28.1)
Determine whether 97°C tea-brewing water is achievable at the reduced atmospheric pressure of a mountain summit (Ex.28.2)
Deduce the latent heat of fusion of ice from the melting-line slope, and estimate lake ice-thickening rates via a thermal-conduction argument (Ex.28.3)
Derive the general L(T) relation for a phase boundary, and a condition for liquid condensing out during adiabatic expansion of saturated vapour (Ex.28.4)
Deduce water's latent heat of evaporation from vapour-pressure-vs-temperature data, and estimate the ice–water equilibrium pressure at −2°C from ice's buoyancy (Ex.28.5)
Show why skate-pressure melting of ice is not the real explanation for ice-skating's low friction (Ex.28.6)
Implement the Metropolis algorithm for the two-dimensional Ising model (Ex.28.7)
Exchange operator P̂12ψ(r1,r2)=ψ(r2,r1); since [Ĥ,P̂12]=0 and |ψ|² must be exchange-invariant, ψ must be an eigenstate of P̂12 with eigenvalue ±1
Bosons (symmetric wavefunction, +1) vs. fermions (antisymmetric, −1); the spin-statistics theorem links this to integer vs. half-integer spin (Example 29.1)

In 2D (unlike 3D), exchange paths can wind around the origin an integer number of times, allowing any phase θ — giving rise to anyons with fractional statistics, relevant to the fractional quantum Hall effect

Two-particle two-state system compared across distinguishable, indistinguishable-classical, indistinguishable-boson, and indistinguishable-fermion cases — bosons allow a symmetric entangled combination, fermions only the antisymmetric one, reducing the accessible state count (Example 29.2)
The Pauli exclusion principle follows directly from antisymmetry: P̂12|φ⟩|φ⟩=−|φ⟩|φ⟩ forces |φ⟩|φ⟩=0, so two fermions cannot occupy the same state

Grand partition function for a single state with occupation n: Z=Σn e^(nβ(μ−E)); restricting n∈{0,1} for fermions gives Z=1+e^(β(μ−E)), while n∈{0,1,2,...} for bosons gives Z=1/(1−e^(β(μ−E))) (geometric series)
Mean occupation ⟨n⟩=−(1/β)(∂lnZ/∂E)=1/(e^(β(E−μ))±1) (+ fermions, − bosons), generalizing directly to a many-state system where the grand partition function factorizes over states (Example 29.3)
The Fermi–Dirac distribution f(E)=1/(e^(β(E−μ))+1) and the Bose–Einstein distribution f(E)=1/(e^(β(E−μ))−1)
Both distributions reduce to the classical Boltzmann factor e^(−β(E−μ)) when β(E−μ)≫1 (low density, negligible multiple occupancy); they differ sharply at high density

The Bose–Einstein distribution diverges as E→μ from above, so μ must always lie below the lowest single-particle energy level for a bosonic system — a constraint with major consequences for quantum gases
Differentiate Bose–Einstein vs. Fermi–Dirac statistics with examples (Ex.29.1)
Find the probability that both particles are in the |0⟩ state for the four cases of Example 29.2 (Ex.29.2)
Rewrite the Fermi–Dirac function in tanh form, show it is symmetric about E=μ, and find its limits for E≪μ, E≫μ, and E≈μ (Ex.29.3)
Determine whether identical particles are always indistinguishable (Ex.29.4)
Estimate the rotational level spacing for para-hydrogen, derive the ortho:para population ratio, and evaluate it at 50K (Ex.29.5)
Derive Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein statistics from the microcanonical ensemble via combinatorial counting and Lagrange multipliers (Ex.29.6)
Grand partition function for non-interacting particles with spin S factorizes over single-particle states, Z=Π_k Zk^(2S+1), Zk=(1±e^(−β(Ek−μ)))^(±1)

Grand potential ΦG=∓kBT(2S+1)Σ_k ln(1±e^(−β(Ek−μ))), converted to an energy integral using the density of states g(E)∝E^(1/2); integrating by parts gives ΦG in terms of ∫E^(3/2)/(e^(β(E−μ))±1)dE (Example 30.1)
Mean occupation nk=1/(e^(β(Ek−μ))±1); N and U follow as integrals over g(E) weighted by this occupation, with the fugacity defined as z=e^(βμ)
These integrals reduce to polylogarithm functions Lin(z), giving N=(2S+1)V/λth³[∓Li3/2(∓z)] and U=(3/2)NkBT Li5/2(∓z)/Li3/2(∓z); also ΦG=−(2/3)U always
In the classical (ideal-gas) limit z≪1, Lin(z)≈z, recovering N∝z, U=(3/2)NkBT, and ΦG=−NkBT=−pV — ordinary equipartition and the ideal gas law (Example 30.2)
The Fermi energy EF=μ(T=0), the energy of the highest occupied state at T=0; at T=0 the occupation is a step function nk=θ(EF−Ek)
Counting states up to kF gives N=(2S+1)V kF³/6π², so kF=[6π²n/(2S+1)]^(1/3) and EF=(ℏ²/2m)[6π²n/(2S+1)]^(2/3); specialized to spin-1/2 (Example 30.3)

At finite T, the sharp step in f(E) is smoothed over a width ~kBT around μ; for real metals EF is several eV (TF of tens of thousands of K), so electrons remain deeply "degenerate" at all ordinary temperatures
T=0 electron-gas pressure p=2U/3V and bulk modulus B=(2/3)nEF, computed from ⟨E⟩=(3/5)EF and U=n⟨E⟩ — giving results of the right order of magnitude for real metals
The Sommerfeld expansion — an asymptotic low-T expansion of ∫φ(E)f(E)dE in powers of (kBT/μ)² — is used to derive the temperature dependence of μ(T) and correct N, U at low T (Example 30.4)
Heat capacity of a degenerate electron gas, CV=(π²/2)NkB(kBT/EF) — linear in T, and dominant over the phonon T³ contribution at sufficiently low temperature (Example 30.5)

The Fermi surface (the constant-energy surface at μ in k-space) is what makes a material a metal; if μ falls in a gap between bands there is no Fermi surface, and the material is a semiconductor or insulator
For a Bose gas, N=(2S+1)V Li3/2(z)/λth³ and U=(3/2)NkBT Li5/2(z)/Li3/2(z); at μ=0 (z=1) these reduce to Riemann zeta functions, Lin(1)=ζ(n) (Example 30.6)
Re-deriving the photon gas's U=π²V(kBT)⁴/15ℏ³c³ from this same formalism (using E=ℏkc and 2 polarization states), recovering the Stefan–Boltzmann result of Ch.23 (Example 30.7)

For bosons with a gapless quadratic dispersion, μ must be negative (else the E=0 state would have infinite occupation), so 0<z<1; but nλth³/(2S+1)=Li3/2(z) has no solution once nλth³/(2S+1) exceeds ζ(3/2)≈2.612 — a puzzle demanding resolution

The puzzle is resolved by recognizing that the sum-to-integral approximation breaks down once the ground state becomes macroscopically occupied, defining a critical temperature kBTc=(2πℏ²/m)[n/(2.612(2S+1))]^(2/3)
Splitting N=N0+N1 (ground-state + excited-state populations) and setting z=1 for T≤Tc gives n1/n=(T/Tc)^(3/2) and hence the condensate fraction n0/n=1−(T/Tc)^(3/2)

Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) is a macroscopic occupation of the single lowest-energy state ("condensation" in momentum/k-space, not real space), driven purely by quantum statistics rather than interactions
Internal energy below Tc, U=0.77NkBTc(T/Tc)^(5/2) (only excited states carry energy, since the condensate sits at E=0) (Example 30.8)

Estimating Tc≈3.1K for liquid ⁴He from its mass and density, remarkably close to the observed 2.2K superfluid transition — though ⁴He is strongly interacting, so the simple non-interacting theory is only qualitatively right (Example 30.9)
Ultracold trapped alkali-atom gases (laser-cooled to ~10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸K) are a much cleaner realization of BEC, directly imaged via the momentum distribution (Cornell/Wieman/Ketterle, 2001 Nobel Prize)

Superfluidity in ⁴He and superconductivity in metals (via bosonic Cooper pairs, BCS theory) are related condensation phenomena — BEC itself requires bosons, so fermionic electrons must first pair up into Cooper pairs to condense
Show that in the classical limit, the fugacity z is the ratio of the thermal volume to the volume per particle of a single-spin excitation (Ex.30.1)
Derive the T=0 Fermi-gas pressure p=(2/5)nEF (Ex.30.2)
Derive the Sommerfeld chemical-potential correction μ(T)=EF−(π²/6)(kBT)²g'(EF)/g(EF) for a general density of states (Ex.30.3)
Derive the heat capacity of a non-interacting Bose gas above and below Tc (Ex.30.4)
Show that Bose–Einstein condensation does not occur in two dimensions (Ex.30.5)
Determine whether the first excited state is also macroscopically occupied in BEC (Ex.30.6)
Sound speed vs=√(B/ρ), where the bulk modulus B=−V(∂p/∂V) (defined positive since pressure increase reduces volume); equivalently B=ρ(∂p/∂ρ)
Isothermal bulk modulus of an ideal gas, BT=−V(∂p/∂V)_T=p (from pV=constant at fixed T)
Isothermal sound speed vs=√(p/ρ)=√(⟨v²⟩/3)=√⟨vx²⟩ — comparable to the mean molecular speed in one direction, consistent with molecular collisions mediating sound
Adiabatic bulk modulus of an ideal gas, BS=−V(∂p/∂V)_S=γp (from pVγ=constant)
Adiabatic sound speed vs=√(γp/ρ)=√(γ⟨v²⟩/3), a factor √γ faster than the isothermal value
Adiabatic sound speed in terms of temperature, vs=√(γkBT/m) — depends only on temperature and molecular mass (Example 31.1)
Relativistic-gas sound speed, vs=c/√3, using p=(1/3)ρc² (Example 31.2)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Are sound waves in general adiabatic or isothermal?
learningPoints.description: Whether sound is adiabatic or isothermal depends on whether heat can diffuse across a compression/rarefaction faster than the wave oscillates; compare the sound wavelength λ=2πvs/ω (∝ω⁻¹) to the thermal skin depth δ (∝ω⁻¹ᐟ²) at the same frequency

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Are sound waves in general adiabatic or isothermal?
learningPoints.description: At ordinary frequencies λ>δ, so sound waves are adiabatic in practice — the isothermal regime would require wavelengths shorter than the mean free path, which is unphysical

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the speed of sound within fluids
learningPoints.description: The continuity equation ∂(ρu)/∂x=−∂ρ/∂t (1D), from mass-flux conservation via the divergence theorem — directly analogous to the diffusion-equation derivation

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the speed of sound within fluids
learningPoints.description: The Euler equation −(1/ρ)∂p/∂x=∂u/∂t+u∂u/∂x, from the pressure-gradient force per unit mass and the convective derivative

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Derivation of the speed of sound within fluids
learningPoints.description: Linearizing both equations (dropping second-order terms in the perturbations u, s=δρ/ρ) and combining them gives the 1D wave equation ∂²s/∂x²=(ρ/B)∂²s/∂t², whose travelling-wave solutions give vs=√(B/ρ)
Estimate the speed of sound in air at aircraft cruising altitude (−60°C) from its value at 0°C (Ex.31.1)
Calculate the speed of sound in nitrogen at 200°C (Ex.31.2)
Estimate sound wavelength and thermal skin depth at 1Hz and 20kHz, confirming sound is adiabatic, and find the crossover frequency where δ=λ (Ex.31.3)
Explain the relative speed of sound in air, hydrogen, and CO2 from their molecular masses (Ex.31.4)
Explain the (illusory) "helium voice" effect (Ex.31.5)
Estimate the time for a sound wave to cross the Sun (Ex.31.6)
Mach number M=w/vs (ratio of disturbance speed to local sound speed); M>1 means supersonic, producing a conical shock front (sonic boom) whose semi-angle decreases as M increases

A shock front is treated as a mathematical discontinuity; in the shock's rest frame, upstream (unshocked, supersonic) gas flows in at v1 and downstream (shocked, subsonic) gas flows out at v2<v1; "strong" vs. "weak" shocks are distinguished by how far w exceeds vs1
The three conservation laws across a shock front (in the shock frame): mass flux ρ1v1=ρ2v2=Φm; momentum flux p1+ρ1v1²=p2+ρ2v2²; energy flux p1v1+(ρ1ũ1+½ρ1v1²)v1=p2v2+(ρ2ũ2+½ρ2v2²)v2
Algebraic combination of the mass and momentum conservation laws gives Φm²=(p2−p1)/(ρ1⁻¹−ρ2⁻¹) and v1²−v2²=(p2−p1)(ρ1⁻¹+ρ2⁻¹) (Example 32.1)
Combining all three conservation laws with the ideal-gas internal energy ũ=p/[(γ−1)ρ] yields the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions: p2/p1=[2γM1²−(γ−1)]/(γ+1) and ρ2/ρ1=v1/v2=(γ+1)M1²/[2+(γ−1)M1²]
As M1→∞, ρ2/ρ1 and v1/v2 saturate (e.g. to 4 and 1/4 for a monatomic gas, γ=5/3) while p2/p1 grows without bound (Examples 32.2–32.3)

The second law of thermodynamics forbids "expansive" shocks (which would convert internal energy into bulk kinetic energy while decreasing entropy) and permits only compressive shocks (M1>1, p2>p1, ρ2>ρ1, T2>T1) — a shock always heats and compresses the gas, converting ordered kinetic energy into random thermal energy

Entropy jump across a shock, ΔS=CV ln{[2γM1²−(γ−1)]/(γ+1) · ([2+(γ−1)M1²]/((γ+1)M1²))^γ}, obtained by substituting the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions into S=CV ln(p/ργ)+const; ΔS>0 always, confirming shocks are irreversible
Show the shock-cone semi-angle is sin⁻¹(1/M) (Ex.32.1)
Derive T2/T1 from the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions and its strong-shock limit (Ex.32.2)
Find the strong-shock limits of ρ2/ρ1, p2/p1, T2/T1 for a monatomic gas (Ex.32.3)
Find the same limits for a diatomic gas such as air (γ=7/5) (Ex.32.4)
Find the strong-shock limit of the entropy increase ΔS (Ex.32.5)
The Langevin equation for a Brownian particle, m dv/dt=−αv+F(t), combining frictional damping α with a zero-mean random force F(t)
Solving for ⟨x²⟩ via the identity d(x·ẋ)/dt=x·ẍ+ẋ² and equipartition ((1/2)m⟨ẋ²⟩=(1/2)kBT) gives ⟨x²⟩=2kBTt/α at long times (t≫m/α), identifying the diffusion constant D=kBT/α (Example 33.1)
D=kBT/α connects the random-fluctuation diffusion rate to the frictional damping/mobility α⁻¹ (the same α that would set the terminal velocity under a steady force); D is independent of mass
The velocity autocorrelation function ⟨v(0)v(t)⟩=⟨v²⟩e^(−αt/m) decays at the same rate the velocity itself relaxes (Example 33.2)
Johnson noise ⟨V²⟩=4kBTRΔf across a resistor, from equipartition applied to transmission-line modes (kBT per mode) balanced against the power dissipated ⟨I²R⟩

Johnson noise is another fluctuation-dissipation example, linking fluctuating noise power to the dissipative resistance R; the quantum version replaces kBT with the mean quantum-oscillator energy ℏω/(e^(βℏω)−1)
In the microcanonical ensemble, Taylor-expanding S(x,E) about its maximum (equilibrium) gives a Gaussian probability distribution p(x)∝exp[−(Δx)²/2⟨(Δx)²⟩], with ⟨(Δx)²⟩=−kB(∂²S/∂x²)⁻¹
Applying this to x=U at fixed V gives ⟨(ΔU)²⟩=kBT²CV (Example 33.3)
Since C∝N and U∝N, fractional energy fluctuations scale as N^(−1/2) — negligible for macroscopic systems, but fluctuations diverge at a critical point (where CV→∞) even for large N
Generalizing the availability A=U−T0S+p0V−μ0N to allow particle exchange gives dStot=−dA/T0, so equilibrium (maximum Stot) corresponds to minimizing A
Taylor-expanding A(x) about its minimum gives the general fluctuation formula ⟨(Δx)²⟩=kBT0/(∂²A/∂x²)
Applying this to volume fluctuations at fixed T,N gives ⟨(ΔV)²⟩=−kBT(∂V/∂p)_T,N; for an ideal gas this reduces to ⟨(ΔV)²⟩=V²/N, i.e. fractional fluctuations ∝N^(−1/2) (Example 33.4)
Analogous fluctuation formulas exist for other conjugate pairs, e.g. ⟨(ΔT)²⟩=kBT²/CV, ⟨(ΔS)²⟩=kBCp, ⟨(Δp)²⟩=kBTκS/CV
Linear response ⟨x(t)⟩_f=∫χ(t−t')f(t')dt' for conjugate variables x,f (product has units of energy); in Fourier space this convolution becomes a simple product, ⟨x̃(ω)⟩_f=χ̃(ω)f̃(ω)
The real part of χ̃(ω) is the in-phase (elastic) response; the imaginary part χ̃''(ω) is the out-of-phase response and corresponds to dissipation (energy absorbed at rate f(t)ẋ(t))
Causality (χ(t)=0 for t<0) forces the real and imaginary parts of χ̃(ω) to be related by the Kramers–Kronig relations, derived via the Fourier transform of the Heaviside step function
The static susceptibility χ̃'(0) (the zero-frequency response) is related by a Kramers–Kronig relation to an integral of the dissipative part χ̃''(ω) over all frequencies
Response function of a damped harmonic oscillator, χ̃(ω)=(1/m)[1/(ω0²−ω²−iωγ)], verifying the static-susceptibility Kramers–Kronig relation explicitly (Example 33.5)

The autocorrelation function Cxx(t)=⟨x(0)x(t)⟩ and the power spectral density ⟨|x̃(ω)|²⟩, related by the Wiener–Khinchin theorem: the power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function
Parseval's theorem, ⟨x²⟩=(1/2π)∫C̃xx(ω)dω — the same total "power" whether computed in the time or frequency domain
A delta-correlated random force ⟨F(t)F(t')⟩=Aδ(t−t') has a flat (frequency-independent) power spectrum (Example 33.6)

Applying this to the Langevin equation recovers the velocity autocorrelation ⟨v(0)v(t)⟩=⟨v²⟩e^(−αt/m) via Fourier methods, and fixes the noise strength A=2αkBT by matching to equipartition (Example 33.7)

For a harmonic system E=(1/2)αx², combining the Boltzmann distribution under an applied force f with the definition of the static susceptibility gives ⟨x²⟩=kBTχ̃'(0), directly connecting equilibrium fluctuations to the response function
The (classical) fluctuation-dissipation theorem, C̃xx(ω)=2kBTχ̃''(ω)/ω, unifying the previous special cases (Johnson noise, Brownian diffusion) as one general relation
Verifying the fluctuation-dissipation theorem explicitly for the damped harmonic oscillator (Example 33.8) and for Johnson noise via a resistor-capacitor circuit model (Example 33.9)
The quantum-mechanical fluctuation-dissipation theorem replaces kBT with the mean energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator, ℏω coth(βℏω/2)/2, recovering the classical result at high temperature
Show that fluctuations at fixed T,N,p follow p(x)∝e^(−G(x)/kBT) (Ex.33.1)
Show the average power dissipated by a sinusoidal force is (1/2)f0²ωχ''(ω) (Ex.33.2)

Writing ds in terms of generalized densities ρk (energy, particle number, charge) and their conjugate potentials φk=∂s/∂ρk, each obeying its own continuity equation
Local entropy production rate Σ=∂s/∂t+∇·Js=Σ_k ∇φk·Jk, obtained by combining the entropy-current definition Js=Σφk Jk with the continuity equations for each ρk
Linear-response relation between generalized currents and forces, Ji=Σj Lij∇φj, defining the kinetic coefficients Lij
Ordinary heat conduction J=−κ∇T cast into this form as Ju=Luu∇(1/T) with Luu=κT² (Example 34.1)
Σ=Σij ∇φi Lij ∇φj≥0 (local entropy production non-negative) requires Lij to be a positive-definite matrix
The Onsager reciprocal relations, Lij=Lji, are an additional symmetry constraint on the kinetic coefficients (stated here, proved in the next section)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Proof of the Onsager reciprocal relations
learningPoints.description: Near equilibrium, expanding the entropy fluctuation ΔS to quadratic order in the departures αk=ρk−ρk^eq gives a Gaussian probability P(α)∝exp(ΔS/kB), with ΔS=−(1/2)Σgijαiαj

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Proof of the Onsager reciprocal relations
learningPoints.description: From this Gaussian, ⟨(∂S/∂αi)αj⟩=−kBδij and hence ⟨αiαj⟩=kB(g⁻¹)ij — a fluctuation formula in the multivariate case, generalizing Ch.33's single-variable result

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Proof of the Onsager reciprocal relations
learningPoints.description: ⟨ΔS⟩=−mkB/2 for m fluctuating degrees of freedom, consistent with equipartition since the mean thermal energy mkBT/2 equals −T⟨ΔS⟩ (Example 34.2)

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Proof of the Onsager reciprocal relations
learningPoints.description: The principle of microscopic reversibility (forward and reverse microscopic processes occur equally often on average) implies the correlation-function symmetry ⟨αi(0)αj(t)⟩=⟨αi(t)αj(0)⟩

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Proof of the Onsager reciprocal relations
learningPoints.description: Differentiating this symmetry at t=0 and substituting the macroscopic kinetic-coefficient relation α̇i=Σk Lik∂S/∂αk yields the Onsager reciprocal relations Lij=Lji

Two dissimilar metals in contact at a common temperature equilibrate their chemical potentials (μA=μB), so the electromotive field combines the electric field and the chemical-potential gradient, E=E+(1/e)∇μ, which is what a voltmeter actually measures

Coupled current relations Je=LEE E+LET∇T and JQ=LTE E+LTT∇T; with no temperature gradient, LEE=σ (electrical conductivity) and the Peltier coefficient Π=LTE/LEE relates heat current to charge current (the Peltier effect)
At a junction between two metals with different Peltier coefficients, an electrical current produces a discontinuous heat-current jump ΠAB Je — the basis of Peltier cooling/heating

With no electrical current, JQ=−κ∇T (thermal conductivity) and E=ε∇T defines the Seebeck coefficient (thermopower) ε=−LET/LEE — a temperature gradient produces an electric field (the Seebeck effect), observable via a thermocouple's Seebeck emf between two dissimilar metals
Thermal conductivity in terms of the L-coefficients, κ=−(LEELTT−LTELET)/LEE, from combining the Seebeck relation with the JQ current equation (Example 34.3)
Applying the Onsager relation LET=LTE (in properly rescaled variables) yields Thomson's second relation, Π=Tε, directly linking the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients

If ε is temperature dependent, an electric current in a single metal (no junction needed) liberates or absorbs Thomson heat, with Thomson coefficient τ=T dε/dT; combined with Thomson's second relation this gives Thomson's first relation, dΠAB/dT+εA−εB=τA−τB

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Time reversal and the arrow of time
learningPoints.description: The Onsager relations rest on microscopic reversibility (time-symmetric underlying dynamics), yet the second law demands entropy always increases — a tension between reversible microscopic laws and irreversible macroscopic behavior

learningPoints.sectionTitle: Time reversal and the arrow of time
learningPoints.description: Boltzmann's attempted resolution (the H-theorem via molecular chaos/stoßzahlansatz) is undermined by pre-collisional correlations required by time-symmetric dynamics; the more likely origin of time's arrow is the Universe's low-entropy initial (boundary) condition rather than any asymmetry in the microscopic laws themselves
