Gravitational collapse condition: a gas cloud collapses if the magnitude of its gravitational potential energy exceeds its thermal kinetic energy, |Ω|>U
Jeans mass MJ=3kBT/(2GmR), from Ω=−GM²/R and U=(3/2)NkBT; equivalently expressed as a Jeans length or Jeans density (Example 35.1)
Equation of hydrostatic equilibrium, dp/dr=−Gm(r)ρ(r)/r², from balancing the pressure-gradient force and gravitational attraction on a thin spherical shell
Using pVγ=constant (adiabatic), internal energy U=pV/(γ−1), so energy density u=p/(γ−1); specialized to non-relativistic (γ=5/3, u=(3/2)p) and relativistic (γ=4/3, u=3p) gases (Example 35.2)
Integrating r³(dp/dr) over the star (using hydrostatic equilibrium) gives the virial theorem ⟨p⟩V=−Ω/3, equivalently 3(γ−1)U+Ω=0

Combining with E=U+Ω gives E=(4−3γ)U; for non-relativistic gas (γ=5/3), E=−U<0 — a bound star with "negative heat capacity" (it heats up as it radiates energy); for relativistic gas (γ=4/3), E=0 — marginally/not stably bound (Example 35.3)

Stars are powered by nuclear fusion ("burning"); the PP chain converts 4 hydrogen nuclei into 1 helium nucleus, releasing 26.5 MeV; heavier elements form via further cycles (e.g. the CNO cycle) up to iron
Estimating the Sun's nuclear lifetime from the ~0.8% mass-defect of hydrogen-to-iron fusion, t~0.008M⊙c²/L⊙~10¹¹ years, consistent with the Sun's actual age
Radiative heat flux modelled as photon diffusion, J=−κ_photon∇T, with κ_photon=(1/3)Cl⟨c⟩ from kinetic theory (C=photon-gas heat capacity per volume, l=photon mean free path, ⟨c⟩=speed of light)
Photon mean free path l=1/(κλρ) from the radiative-transfer/absorption equation dIλ=−κλρIλds (opacity κλ)

Combining these gives the stellar temperature-gradient equation dT/dr=−3κ(r)ρ(r)L(r)/(64πr²σT(r)³), completing the four coupled equations of stellar structure (mass, hydrostatic equilibrium, luminosity, temperature)
Condition for convective instability, |dT/dr|>(1−1/γ)(T/p)|dp/dr|, from comparing the adiabatic density change of a rising parcel to the ambient density gradient (Schwarzschild criterion)

The principle of homology: a star's structure scales self-similarly with its total mass M and radius R, so pressure/temperature/density profiles at any fractional radius scale by the same overall factors
Homology scaling gives p∝M²R⁻⁴ and T∝MR⁻¹ from the hydrostatic-equilibrium and ideal-gas-law equations (Example 35.4)

Combining these with a density/temperature-dependent opacity (Kramers opacity κ∝ρT⁻³·⁵ for low-mass stars, or constant κ for massive/electron-scattering-dominated stars) gives the mass-luminosity relations L∝M^5.5/R^0.5 (low-mass) and L∝M³ (high-mass) (Example 35.5)

The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (luminosity vs. effective temperature) shows the main sequence (hydrogen-burning stars, empirically L∝M^3.5) and the red-giant branch (post-main-sequence stars with an inert helium core and an expanded, cooler envelope); stellar lifetime scales as M^(1−a), so more massive stars burn through their fuel faster

Relating electron number density to stellar density via charge neutrality, n≈Zρ/(Amp), gives p_electron∝ρ^(5/3)
Balancing p_electron∝ρ^(5/3) against the gravitational pressure p_grav∝ρ^(4/3) (from the virial theorem, Ω=−3GM²/5R) gives a stable equilibrium density (Example 36.1)
White-dwarf mass-radius relation R∝M^(−1/3), from combining the equilibrium density condition (ρ∝M²) with ρ∝M/R³

The Chandrasekhar limit M≈1.4M⊙, the mass above which electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support a white dwarf, from requiring the Fermi momentum to reach mec

Above the Chandrasekhar limit, non-relativistic neutron degeneracy pressure (∝ρ^(5/3), following the same scaling as electrons but weaker since neutrons are heavier) can support a neutron star, via the equilibrium n⇌p⁺+e⁻+ν̄e favouring neutrons at high density
Minimum rotation period of a neutron star, τ=2π√(R³/GM), from balancing gravitational and centrifugal forces at the equator (Example 36.3)
The maximum neutron-star mass (~5M⊙, by analogy with the Chandrasekhar limit) above which neutrons become relativistic and the star becomes unstable (Example 36.4)
Escape velocity vesc=√(2GM/R) from energy balance; the Schwarzschild radius RS=2GM/c² is where vesc=c

Black holes are not perfectly "black" — infalling matter is ripped apart and radiates before crossing the event horizon (powering luminous active galactic nuclei), and quantum vacuum fluctuations near the horizon produce Hawking radiation

The Hawking temperature kBTH=ℏc³/8πGM (a black hole has a well-defined black-body temperature that rises as it loses mass); estimating the evaporation lifetime from dM/dt·c²=−4πRS²σTH⁴ gives a lifetime ∝M³, so small black holes evaporate much faster than large ones
The Eddington luminosity limit Ledd=4πGMc/κ, from balancing inward gravitational force against outward radiation pressure on infalling matter
The corresponding Eddington accretion rate Ṁedd=4πcR/κ, from L=GMṀ/R
Black-hole entropy S=kB A/4lP² (Bekenstein-Hawking entropy), where A=4πRS² is the horizon area and lP=√(Gℏ/c³) is the Planck length; one bit of information corresponds to four Planck areas
Black-hole entropy (and hence area) can only increase classically, consistent with the second law; but this makes entropy scale with area rather than volume, unlike ordinary extensive entropy
Bekenstein's generalized second law: the sum of ordinary matter entropy plus black-hole entropy never decreases, even when matter falling into a black hole seems to "lose" its own entropy

Earth is in radiative balance (incoming visible/UV photons from the Sun ≈ outgoing infrared photons), but since the entropy per photon is roughly frequency-independent, the fewer high-energy incoming photons carry less entropy than the many low-energy outgoing photons — so the Sun supplies Earth (and life) with a flux of low-entropy energy

The Sun's own low entropy ultimately derives from the unthermalized gravitational degrees of freedom in the early Universe, which provided the low-entropy reservoir that drives gravitational collapse and stellar/biological complexity

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The temperature profile in the atmosphere
learningPoints.description: The troposphere is convectively unstable when the actual temperature gradient exceeds Γ (warm air below, cool air above), driving convection (and, combined with the Coriolis force, cyclones/anticyclones); above the tropopause, the stratosphere is stably stratified and roughly isothermal in its lower part

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The temperature profile in the atmosphere
learningPoints.description: A two-layer radiative model of the stratosphere — absorbing a fraction ε of the Earth's outgoing IR and re-emitting from both faces — gives Tstrat=TE/2^(1/4)≈214K, matching observed lower-stratosphere temperatures

learningPoints.sectionTitle: The temperature profile in the atmosphere
learningPoints.description: Temperature rises again higher in the stratosphere (ozone UV absorption), falls in the mesosphere, then rises sharply in the thermosphere (energetic solar photons/cosmic rays)

Extinction coefficient κν and the Beer-Lambert law Iν(z)=Iν(0)e^(−κνρaz) for radiance passing through a uniform absorbing medium; more generally Iν(z)=Iν(0)e^(−χν) with optical path length χν=∫κνρa ds
Optically thick (χ≫1, opaque) vs. optically thin (χ≪1, transparent) regimes

The radiative-transfer (Schwarzschild) equation dIν/dχν+Iν=Jν, generalizing Beer-Lambert to include reradiation via the source function Jν (=Bν(T) in local thermal equilibrium, since "good absorbers are good emitters")
Irradiance F (power per unit area, integrated over a hemisphere of directions) vs. radiance I; for isotropic radiation F=πI, and for black-body radiation F(T)=σT⁴=πB(T) (Example 37.2)
The diffuse approximation reduces the 3D transfer problem to a 1D equation in a scaled optical depth χ*, dF/dχ*+F=πB (downward) or −dF/dχ*+F=πB (upward)

Solving the upward-irradiance equation gives F(χ)=πB(χs)−π∫dB/dχ'[1−e^(−(χ'−χ))]dχ' — the outgoing irradiance equals the surface blackbody emission reduced by absorption/reemission from the colder atmosphere above (Example 37.3)
The Earth absorbs short-wavelength (visible/UV) solar radiation and re-emits long-wavelength (infrared) radiation, since its temperature is far lower than the Sun's

Homonuclear diatomic molecules (N2, O2) have no infrared-active vibrational modes (no dipole-moment change), so they don't absorb IR; heteronuclear/bent molecules (CO2, H2O) have infrared-active modes and strongly absorb specific IR wavelengths — these are the greenhouse gases

Greenhouse gases absorb and reradiate IR that would otherwise escape directly to space, acting as a "winter coat" that raises the surface temperature — necessary for habitability in the right amount, but harmful in excess

Applying the radiative-transfer result to an idealized exponential density/optical-depth profile (scale height h=H/2) shows the outgoing irradiance decreases logarithmically with the absorber-concentration multiplier α, ΔF≈−πΓhB1 ln α (Example 37.4)
Anthropogenic climate change: rising CO2 concentrations from fossil-fuel combustion are driving measurable global warming

Positive feedback: warmer air holds more water vapour (itself a greenhouse gas) before saturation, amplifying warming; reduced ice cover also lowers Earth's albedo, absorbing more solar energy — both outweigh negative feedbacks (e.g. increased plant CO2 uptake)

The oceans' large heat capacity and CO2's long atmospheric relaxation time mean substantial warming is already "committed" even if emissions stopped immediately, and future projections remain uncertain due to population, industrialization, and cloud-cover unknowns
